speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should like to inform the house of certain changes in the ministry on the occasion of the union of Canada and Newfoundland. Hon. James A. MacKinnon has resigned as Minister of Mines and Resources and has been sworn in as a minister without portfolio. He remains a member of the treasury board, and also Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce and Acting Minister of Mines and Resources.
Before announcing the further changes I should like to read to the house Mr. MacKinnon's letter of resignation and my reply. The letter from Mr. MacKinnon is as follows:
Minister of Mines and Resources Canada
Ottawa, Ontario, March 21, 1949.
Dear Mr. St. Laurent:
I have been thinking further along the lines of our recent conversation in which I informed you that my doctor advised me that I should, under no circumstances, consider seeking re-election to the House of Commons. I believe I should now make a public announcement to our friends in Edmonton West, so that they may be able to give immediate consideration to the choice of a candidate to contest the next general election. If you approve, I shall advise the Liberals of Edmonton West accordingly this week end.	.
I have been very happy to be associated with the government responsible for completing the work of the Fathers of Confederation, bringing to a successful conclusion the union with Newfoundland. As
you know, I have been looking forward to being relieved of onerous departmental duties. I might make a further contribution to the harmonious completion of the union with Newfoundland by placing my portfolio at your disposal at this time.
It is, of course, going to be a wrench to sever my connection with a government I have been so happily associated with for so many years, but even apart from the state of my health, I feel it is desirable to keep bringing new blood into the administration, as we have been doing steadily for some years, in order to maintain the combination of experience and youthful energy which has enabled the party to serve Canada so well over the years.
I should be glad, therefore, if you would feel perfectly free to act on this suggestion of mine if it will lit in with your plans.
May I repeat here what I said to you personally- how proud and happy I am to have been associated for so many years with our late leader, Mr. King, and just recently under your own great leadership.
Assuring you of my continuing admiration and loyalty, I am,
Yours faithfully,
Jas. A. MacKinnon
To this letter I replied as follows:
Office of the Prime Minister Canada
Ottawa,
March 23, 1949.
Hon. James A. MacKinnon, M.P.,
Minister of Mines and Resources,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. MacKinnon:
I am grateful for your characteristically generous letter of March 21. No one can regret more than I do that your health will no longer permit you to face the rigours of a campaign for re-election to the House of Commons, particularly as your retirement will remove one of the small band of colleagues who have been with me since the first day I appeared in the council chamber.
At the same time, I know how arduous and devoted your services have been and how greatly you deserve some relief from the exacting responsibilities you have borne so long and with such distinction.
I agree, therefore, that it would be advisable to make an announcement now of your intention not to be a candidate in the next general elections.
Like you, I am impressed with the importance of doing everything we can to make the people of Newfoundland feel their province is a full partner from the first day of union. Your readiness to make your portfolio available will enable me to make certain rearrangements which will ensure full representation of Newfoundland in the ministry. I am sure all Canadians will be grateful for your patriotic suggestion that you make this personal contribution to the success of the new union.
I am going to ask you, however, to remain in the government as a minister without portfolio at least until the end of the present session. I feel it would be most unfortunate not to have the point of view of Alberta fully represented at the council table in the next few critical months.
It is my hope that the number of supporters of the government who will be returned in Alberta in

The Ministry
the next elections will be such that the only difficulty will be to choose the member who is best qualified to represent the interests and viewpoint of your province in the government of the nation.
I confess, however, it is not going to be easy to find anyone who could serve Alberta and all Canada with greater devotion than you have done over the past decade; and I hope you are going to continue for many years, though with lightened burdens, to contribute of your wisdom and experience to the public interest.
In conclusion, may I thank you again for all the help and encouragement you have given me over the years and, particularly, in these last few difficult months.
With warmest regards,
Yours very sincerely,
Louis S. St. Laurent.

Mr. Speaker, many of us who have been in the house with the hon. member who is now relinquishing his post would like to say that we have appreciated his genial manner, his courtesy and his unfailing friendliness toward all of us.
I do not wish to make any reference to the political implications of the correspondence which has been read, but I do wish to say to Mr. MacKinnon how deeply we regret that he is obliged to retire for reasons of health. We wish him many long years to enjoy the honours that are deservedly his.

Mr. Speaker, I join in the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Inasmuch as the oldest friendship I have-and it is a very personal friendship-among the membership of the house has been with my old friend from Edmonton West, I cannot let this opportunity go by without saying a word about him.
Our friendship goes back a long way. I knew him first when I was a high school student in Regina and he was attending normal school. That makes him older than I, in the normal course of events. I next knew him when I took a hockey club up to Edmonton; and while he did not play hockey, he arranged things so that we did not have a single chance of success. We were defeated. He is the finest wangler-and I do not use that word politically at all-and the greatest arranger of things, with that genial manner, that grand smile, and an outlook which embraces everyone, that I have ever met in my life.
I say to him politically-and in this I pay him the greatest compliment I could pay to anyone in the House of Commons-that we on this side of the house are unanimous in our opinion, one which has become a judgment, that we have always received straight and fine treatment from him, right from the beginning of his holding office until the present time.

I need hardly say that the only difference I have ever had with him has been a political one; and I am content even with that, because he succeeded where he lived, and I succeeded where I lived. I am sure, sir, that all in the House of Commons will agree with me when I say that through his leaving the house will be poorer. And let me add that so far as the welfare of Canada is concerned, it could not have been in better hands than those of my old friend Jim MacKinnon.

Mr. Speaker, as a fellow Albertan I too would like to say just a word of appreciation of the friendship of the hon. member and of many favours he has done for me, though we have been on opposite sides of the house. May I add I have never taken a matter to Mr. MacKinnon which he did not give his utmost attention and most sympathetic consideration.
He has been helpful to me ever since I came to the house. Being comparatively new in the federal field, naturally I had to look to someone to give me help. I must say-and I acknowledge it freely-that I always received most sympathetic assistance from the minister in every way he could possibly give it.
I regret very much the necessity of his having to leave the house and the ministry at this time. Let me add that the people of Alberta generally, without regard to their political affiliations or colour, will definitely regret seeing Jim MacKinnon leave the administration. He has many friends outside the Liberal party, and many friends outside Alberta.
I extend to him sincerely, on behalf of our party in the House of Commons, the kindest possible wishes for many years of happiness and contentment.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps a word from one of those known to be more closely associated with the urban population of our country might be in order. For a quarter of a century it has been my privilege and pleasure to know Mr. MacKinnon. In those days when he sat in this chamber as a private member-a high privilege for anyone to enjoy-I learned to know and respect him. In common with a mutual friend, the late Allan Fraser, secretary-manager of the National Dairy Council of Canada, in other days we were able to ' espouse the cause of the dairy interests in this country.
It runs through my mind now, sir, that once again, when someone must rise in his place and espouse that cause, we know we have a true friend in Mr. MacKinnon. I do not wish to let this opportunity pass without

saying that between 1935 and 1939, and from that time forward, in company with many other thousands of rural citizens of Canada who were interested in the dairy industry, we knew we always had an adviser and friend in Mr. MacKinnon.
Therefore I pay tribute to him on behalf of the rural members of the house, hoping that in the days to come he in turn will see to it that those who are interested in the dairy industry of Canada may find in him a source of advice and warm feeling toward that industry, and that they will know where to turn to get good advice. I am sure he will be ready and willing on all occasions, whether in this chamber or, as is more likely, in the other place, to look after the interests of those whom he served so well from 1935 on.
I pay tribute to Mr. MacKinnon. I have enjoyed his friendship, and I hope he may be spared many years in another place to serve Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I too cannot let this occasion pass without expressing my appreciation of the help the minister has given to me by way of tendering information on the occasions of the many trips I have made into northern Alberta and the Northwest Territories.
Everywhere I have gone in that part of the country I have met friends of James MacKinnon. At different places I heard about his visits to the areas to which I had gone, and learned of the high regard the people in the far north have for him. I am very sorry to hear that his health makes it imperative for him to retire.
I have a particularly warm feeling for my hon. friend for another reason. Before leaving for my last trip to the far north I had expressed to the minister a desire to get from Norman Wells to Whitehorse. Now to get from Norman Wells to Whitehorse by a Canadian plane means that you must fly down to Fort Nelson and then back to Whitehorse. I had inquired from the Canadian Pacific Air Lines what the ticket would cost, and my memory is that it was just under $500. I was quite prepared to pay that, because I wanted to go via Whitehorse to meet my good friend the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) at Dawson.
You can imagine how happy I was when I arrived at Norman Wells from Aklavik to be met by an officer of the United States flying forces. He saluted and said that he was at my service, that he understood that I wanted to go to Whitehorse. At first I refused to accept the trip, having planned to go by Canadian Pacific Air Lines, but when he told me that it would not cost me one dollar, that the plane was at my service, I could hardly refuse. I learned later at Edmonton that the
The Ministry
minister had written to the chief of the United States command, who had sent on the order that saved me just under $500. Therefore, being of Scotch extraction, I want to express to another man of Scotch extraction my warm feelings of appreciation. I do hope that his health will be restored and, as the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) has said, that he will arrive in good health in another place at the far end of this building. After all, that is the anteroom to heaven.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot let this occasion pass without adding my voice to the voices of other hon. members who have expressed friendship and admiration for a man with whom I have been associated for nearly half a century. I do this not only as a member of parliament, and as one who has been associated with the minister in the fight on behalf of Liberalism in Alberta, but as a member of a family with which he has been friendly for years. My wife's family have always had the highest regard for Jim MacKinnon.
I hope that a man of his calibre, of his integrity and of his ability will be found in the ranks of the Liberal party to take his place in the cabinet by the side of the Prime Minister. It is to be regretted that public life has taken so much out of a man whom I have known as strong and virile. It indicates to hon. members of this house what a hard taskmaster politics can be.
I would ask hon. members to bear with me for a moment while I express on behalf of the French Canadians of Alberta, in the language that they speak, their admiration and love for James MacKinnon, in whom they have always had a most true and understanding friend.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, as the representative of close to 50,000 French Canadians in the province of Alberta, I am glad of this opportunity to express in this house the feelings of sincere and deep friendship which they have always entertained for the hon. the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. MacKinnon), and to wish him recovery, on their behalf, so that he may long continue to serve the Liberal party in the other place with the same ability he has displayed during the fifteen years he has spent in this house.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the glowing tributes that have been paid to the hon. minister, I am sure I would be remiss in my duty if I did not convey to him the good feelings that come from his old home place. I appreciate that the west takes credit for having had such a man up in that district, but we in Bruce feel

The Ministry
that we are entitled to the most credit, because that is where the hon. gentleman was born, and I am sure that is where part of his heart is.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKinnon (Minister without portfolio):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, needless to say, this is an entire surprise to me; nevertheless I appreciate these all too flattering comments from the various quarters of this house. I myself particularly like people, and I am deeply touched by what has just been said. I am most grateful.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There are days in public life which are pretty grim, but it is gratifying that there can be occasions such as this when members of all parties feel that it is fitting to recognize deserving public service.
Hon. Colin Gibson has resigned as Secretary of State and been appointed Minister of Mines and Resources.
One of our new fellow Canadians, Hon. F. Gordon Bradley, of the new province of Newfoundland, has been sworn to the privy council and appointed Secretary of State of Canada.
We all rejoice in the completion of that project which has been maturing for so many years. As a mark of recognition of his service to Canada and to Newfoundland, the retiring high commissioner, Mr. Charles J. Burchell, K.C., has this morning been sworn to the Privy Council of Canada.
Before concluding this statement I should like to mention the services of four other gentlemen who have rendered exceptional service in connection with the union we are celebrating today. The first is my predecessor, the right hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Mackenzie King), who was Prime Minister throughout the greater part of the negotiations leading to union, and who had a decisive voice in the decisions taken during that period.
I am sure that all my colleagues who shared in these negotiations will feel that I should mention especially the untiring and devoted services of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) who was vice chairman of the Newfoundland committee, and of my parliamentary assistant, the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris).
I feel that all members of the public service would also agree that special mention should be made of the able and devoted service which has been given day in and day out, and often far into the night, by Dr. R. A. MacKay, of the Department of External Affairs.
As we all rejoice in the completion of confederation, they will have a special satisfaction in the knowledge of a task well done for Newfoundland and for all Canada.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. 188, to amend the Railway Act.

subtopic: CONTROL OF SMOKE AND SOOT FROM ROUNDHOUSES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: CONTROL OF SMOKE AND SOOT FROM ROUNDHOUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to protect the health and property of people living in the vicinity of railway roundhouses. It adds one paragraph to section 287, subsection 1, of the Railway Act, which empowers the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada to specifically require a railway company to install a steam generating system, which is the modern and only completely effective method of preventing the undue emission of smoke and soot
Railway Act Amendment into the atmosphere to the detriment of the surrounding district.
The amendment provides that a municipal council may appeal to the board of transport commissioners, which may take specific action if they deem it warranted under the circumstances. The previous orders did not give the board sufficient power to utilize modern methods of smoke abatement which have been developed since the act was written and the orders of the board passed.
The amendment recognizes the authority of the municipal council, which is empowered to make the request, and authorizes the board of transport commissioners to act if they are satisfied that the situation warrants it.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

I think it is particularly fitting that Canada should be represented by the head of its government. Not only should the occasion be dignified by his presence, but this house should be represented by its senior minister. There is another reason-

It is only a short time ago that the Prime Minister, quite properly and wisely, saw fit to visit the President of the United States during the course of the discussions leading up to the Atlantic pact. As the Atlantic pact is to be dealt with next week, it would be particularly suitable that the Prime Minister of Canada meet the prime ministers of the United Kingdom and the other dominions, and exchange views, with the special advantage he possesses in the knowledge of the views of our great neighbour to the south of us, which will play such an important part in the general discussions.
There is also the fact that with the signing of the North Atlantic pact there will be many matters which should be discussed at the highest governmental level. It is well known to every hon. member of this house that while the written record may contain the formal exchange of opinions between governments, personal exchange of opinion is also of immense importance at a time like this.
I earnestly hope, therefore, that the adoption of this resolution will bring the assurance that the Prime Minister will attend the conference.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: STATEMENT AS TO DEVELOPMENT OF A COMPREHENSIVE HOUSING PROJECT FOR THE CITY OF TORONTO
speechtext:
Yesterday the member for Parkdale (Mr. Timmins) asked if a report could be submitted about the progress being made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the matter of a comprehensive housing project for the city of Toronto and surrounding townships. In answer I might say that despite the fact that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has had many conversations with the mayors of Toronto, not as much progress has been made in the development of a comprehensive program in Toronto and surrounding municipalities as we should like.
The difficulties centre around the lack of land for housing projects in the city of Toronto, and in the provision of services, particularly schools in suburban municipalities. This problem is particularly acute with respect to veterans rental housing. It would have been most desirable to undertake this year the construction of a large number of units for rental to veterans in the Toronto area. But as I said before, despite the fact there have been many conversations, not as much progress has been made as we should like.
With regard to development by private enterprise working with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a number of projects are under way. The largest and most important of these* is a land assembly project in North York. This is being developed by two lending institutions working with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Initially it will provide eight hundred lots for home ownership, and in due course a possible further eight hundred. In addition, some five rental insurance projects are either under way or in the negotiation stage.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to move this resolution upon which a bill will be founded to provide services in the new province of Newfoundland. In this supply bill I am asking for the usual one-sixth of all items and an additional seven-twelfths of two special items which are provided in the schedule to the bill. It relates almost entirely to the sum of $5 million which represents the settlement of various accounts in taking over inventories on the railway and inventories at Gander airport, and a general settlement of accounts between the dominion and the new province as of the date of union. The major portion of that vote will be required in the first month.
The second item relates to special payments which have to be made in connection with airways and the airport at Gander, an additional one-sixth of the fisheries item, the maintenance and extension of the bait service and a special vote for the unemployment insurance commission. I give the usual undertaking, of course, that the passing of these items does not preclude any member from discussing any item of estimates when such item comes up for vote in the regular way.

There is just one question that I should like to ask the minister. By means of this vote of interim supply, one-sixth is provided for in general and in respect of two items a larger amount is to be voted. For the sake of argument, suppose that the House of Commons never arrived at a point before dissolution where all of the supply had been voted? Suppose that one-sixth had been voted by the house and circumstances compelled dissolution, or it was found convenient for the government to have dissolution, which is within the realm of possibility. Is the government then in a position to carry on under governor general's warrants, regardless of the amount that has been voted by parlia-

ment and regardless of the extent of the expenditures which would have to be made under such warrants?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, I read with some interest the article to which my hon. friend has referred. I had not heard of the projects before. The question of the relief of traffic difficulties in Montreal, as of course in other cities, is a matter for the municipal administration of that city, which must assume the responsibility for it, and pay the cost.

The only project I know about at the present time is one of long standing to construct a tunnel under the Lachine canal at St. Remi street. That project has been mooted for years. As the committee knows, the dominion government is responsible for the upkeep of bridges over canals maintained by the dominion government. The tunnel project is one in which, if it is agreed to, part of the cost will be paid by the government and part by the city of Montreal. There is an item in the estimates already tabled providing for the federal contribution to the construction of such a tunnel. May I ask a further question of the Minister of Finance. Yesterday I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare whether any further progress had been made in the matter of paying old age pensions in Newfoundland. As the minister will recall, when we were discussing the legislation having to do with the entry of Newfoundland into Canada, a great deal was said about the delay which was likely to ensue in that matter.
The government took the position that there was nothing the federal government could do to pay old age pensions to persons in Newfoundland until the Newfoundland provincial government had passed the necessary provincial legislation and subsequently entered into an agreement with the federal government. The $2,500 under miscellaneous is for one-quarter of Canada's share of charges in connection with the cost of common services of the British commonwealth scientific office in London. The amount is required for the payment of the Department of Agriculture's share of charges for common services of B.C.S.O. in London, England. The national research council absorbs 50 per cent of all charges, the defence research board 25 per cent, and the Department of Agriculture the remaining 25 per cent. These three payments are Canada's share of the charges for B.C.S.O. The major countries at present participating in this scheme are the United Kingdom, South Africa, Australia, India, New Zealand and Canada. The B.C.S.O. liaison offices maintain services to all participant countries through their liaison officers, and carry on scientific work such as reporting on methods for promoting the utilization of scientific and technical results. The total of Canada's share in the above-mentioned connection is $9,627.29 up to December 31, 1948. I should like to ask the minister if the total of more than one and three-quarter million dollars in the supplementary estimates for his department has already all been spent in the year which ended on the 31st of March. If so, under what authority has the money been spent, not having been voted by parliament? The government now comes along after spending the money, if that is the case, and wants to have it voted.

Of course these votes that are numbered are separate items, and each one of them has to be voted by the house. When we come to the end of a year it will be found that there are small surpluses under some items, and there are deficits in others. This vote is to take care of some of the deficit amounts. It does not necessarily mean that on balance in the department there is $1,761,000 required in addition to what was voted last year. So far as these particular items are concerned we require more. There may be other places in the department where there are surpluses.

I wonder if the minister can tell us what the balance is in the department? Is this amount of money the balance of what was voted and not spent, or is this actually money which was spent without authority?

There is no possibility of saying at this moment what it will be. While the accounts are balanced at the end of March, they are not actually closed until we get pretty well on to the end of April. speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to explain. Possibly he is not aware exactly how government accounts are run. As the Minister of Agriculture has pointed out, individual items are voted, and the votes cannot be transferred. In other words, if you vote $10,000 for science service, and $5,000 for some other service, and you do not spend all your money in science service, and you find your expenditures were more in the other service, you would have to come back and ask for a supplementary. One cannot tell until the government accounts have been closed at the end of the year how one comes out. As I said in my budget address, total expenditures this year will be within one per cent of the estimates last year, but as far as individual items are concerned, they are made up fifteen and sixteen months before the moneys have to be spent, and the purpose of supplemen-taries is to get the house to vote moneys for special purposes where the original estimates have been too low.
I should like to refer to item 569.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Wait till we come to it. Let us take the items in order.

I have a question which might come under any of the items. It is my information that salaries in certain sections of the Department of Agriculture have been in arrears for some six or eight weeks now. Will the minister indicate how general that condition is, whether it is an accidental situation in one year, and what is the reason for it? Unless it is casual labour, I imagine their salaries were pretty well provided for when the estimates were made up.

I do not happen to know of any case where that is true. Salaries are paid in the ordinary way in the department, and I presume they are all paid up to date. There may be some reason for their not being paid at some point, but I do not know what it would be.

I do not like to make this request, but one of the members of our party is attending the meeting of one of the committees of the house. We have sent for him, and I wonder if the minister would mind holding this item open and passing on to the next one.

Very well.
Item stands.
Supply-Agriculture Science service-
565. Science service administration - further amount required, $17,000.

I wonder whether the minister is in a position to give a report on the investigations made by his department in Saskatchewan with relation to the grasshopper infestation. The other day I asked a question on this subject, and the minister indicated the degree to which his department interested itself in this matter. During the last two or three days I have received four letters from various parts of Saskatchewan requesting reconsideration on the part of the Department of Agriculture of the question of assisting the rural municipalities and the provinces in this connection. I speak without scientific knowledge, but from the information I have gained from these farmers and also from the report of the Saskatchewan department, I believe the threat this year to Saskatchewan wheat farming is the most serious that the province has faced in many years. Whether anything can be done at this time by the federal authorities to alleviate or reduce the danger, I cannot say; but I want to point out to the minister how much these municipalities desire any assistance that may be given by the federal department.
In saying that, I am making no indirect criticism of the provincial department of agriculture, because I want to keep this matter entirely removed from any question of partisanship or any difference of view as to the responsibilities of the federal and provincial departments. I know the minister realizes how serious it is, and if the federal authority can do anything to meet this challenge, which has all the appearances of a provincial disaster that will have widespread repercussions throughout the dominion, that should be done even if it results in some material departure from the relative jurisdictions heretofore assumed by federal and provincial authorities.

I am sure the hon. member realizes that no matter how severe the grasshopper infestation may be this year it cannot possibly be any worse than it has been on other occasions in the past; and from experience I can say that it is never as bad in the first year as in the second or third year. There is no information in regard to the movement of grasshoppers and the infestation that has developed, which is not known either to the department here or to the departments in the prairie provinces. The practice always has been and still is, however, that the work referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre is done by the provincial departments. That is not a matter of either criticism or the shifting of responsibility. The responsibility is admitted; there is no question about

Supply-Agriculture
it at all. The detailed information we have with regard to grasshoppers is obtained from the provinces. If there is a movement of grasshoppers across the state of North Dakota, for instance, or elsewhere toward Canada we check with the United States authorities and get all the information we can. So do the provincial people; but we may take a little more responsibility in regard to getting that information because of the international nature of the situation.
As far as attacking the problem is concerned, or dealing with the situation that exists, that is done by the provincial departments through the municipalities, and it has been carried on in that way for years. No one is suggesting that this procedure should be changed. I have not had a single letter about it from anyone; and I would suggest to any hon. member who is getting letters that he write back to the interested individuals immediately, telling them that the place to write is to the provincial department of agriculture at Regina, where they will get all the information available without the least difficulty. If the department at Regina finds that it requires information it has not got but that we can obtain for it, or if they find that we have some scientific personnel who would be useful to them, or if they find that any of our personnel can be utilized to help them, all they need do is say so and that personnel is made available at once. So the quickest way to get results is to have those concerned write directly to the provincial government and get their directions from them. If we started to mix in that we would be likely to complicate the matter rather than help.

Following what the minister has just said, I would point out that a situation might well develop in which the federal government could take some part and some responsibility other than ^ merely making available scientific information. I do not know what policy is being followed in the other provinces, but my understanding is that the government of Saskatchewan is now selling and distributing in bulk form through the municipalities certain liquids which can be used in the boom sprayers for counteracting the grasshopper infestation.
That is the method that has always been followed and is still being followed.

But last year, as the minister well knows, the cost to the farmer was $2 to $3 a gallon, which made the cost per acre very high. This year under the provincial policy I understand it is being distributed at a cost of about 75 cents per

acre. But I believe the minister will agree that even this cost is relatively high for a farmer with a small crop. I was through this difficulty in the thirties, and I realize that even though some farmers may undertake the protection of their own farms, the flight of 'hoppers into a certain area may still destroy their crops, as mine have been destroyed. So I would urge the minister to assist financially by subsidizing the cost of the necessary chemicals, in order to help those provinces which may be facing a calamity through this grasshopper infestation.

Item agreed to.
Administration service-
563. Departmental administration-further amount required, $2,500.

I appreciate very much the kindness of the committee in letting this item stand until I could be here. I had asked to be advised when it was called, but now I find that I have nothing to bring before the committee.

Item agreed to.
567. Plant protection-further amount required, $12,500.
What is this for, in connection with plant protection? Is it just for traveling expenses, or does it cover assistance of any other kind?
It was a traveling expense item entirely.

About $200,000 of the supplementary estimates is for traveling expenses; that is another blank cheque we have to vote. In addition to that there is a sum of $6 million for temporary assistance in the main estimates, another blank cheque we have to give. We are never given a breakdown of these items, but we are still asked to vote a total of $6 million, which is quite a bit of money, without having any information concerning it.

Mr. Chairman, if we turn to page 14 it will be found that it is for traveling expenses, $12,500, in connection with plant protection. The items that are concerned are seed potatoes in Prince Edward Island, bulbs in British Columbia and elm disease in the central provinces. It is a matter of the traveling expenses of those who are called upon to go out and check on these different operations.

Item agreed to.
569. Compensation for animals slaughtered, $100,000.
This item covers $100,000 for animals slaughtered under

the administration of the Health of Animals Act. I should like to ask the minister if the amount of compensation paid for purebred and grade animals slaughtered varies to any extent? Would he be kind enough to give a full explanation of the policy in that regard?

Up to the present the policy has been to pay two-thirds of the maximum valuation which may be placed on the animals. The maximum for grades is $60 and the maximum for purebreds is $150. Only two-thirds of that is paid by way of compensation, so that the maximum amount that can be paid for a grade animal is $40 and the maximum amount for purebreds is $100.
In addition to that, animals which are not condemned outright and which may contain marketable parts return to the person who owned the animal the amount which he gets from the government plus the amount he is paid by the packing house for the marketable parts. In so far as animals that are declared to have T.B. in the greater part of the carcass are concerned, I can well understand that there has been some hardship with prices as high as they have been in recent months. Those people receive very little in addition to what the government pays, and provision is being made to pay more in so far as those animals are concerned.
Has the government come to any decision as to what extra money is to be paid for those condemned animals?

A final decision has not been made and for that reason I am not able to say exactly what it will be. I am able to state that those who are concerned with the matter have been in to see us and they did not ask for any more than we were considering giving, so I think it likely there will be satisfaction when an announcement is finally made.

Will the
minister state who has been interviewing him in that regard? Has it been the cattlemen's association?
No, representatives of the counties that have been concerned with the tests that have been made in recent months.
Have there been representations from western delegates?
There have been people representing western producers, yes.
Have any estimates been made as to what amount will be paid?

The only doubt at the moment is when we shall start payment, that is as to how far back it shall extend. It is
Supply-Agriculture
obvious it must go back to some date, because we have not finished the testing in a number of counties. Some date has to be determined, but I do not expect there is going to be any great difficulty about that. Nevertheless, it has to be determined before I can make an announcement.

Under this item, animals are destroyed when they are infected with tuberculosis. I think that is the only disease that has been discussed by the minister. What other infections or diseases are considered to be of such a serious character that the animal is destroyed?
Cholera in hogs.

I should like to bring to the minister's attention a very important thing, if it has not already been brought to his attention, and that is the fact that in many of these areas, even those in which this system of inspecting cattle is undertaken, the inspection is not efficient. In my own district, in the Carlyle area, a number of residents have become seriously ill from a certain tubercular disease, alleged to have been caused by infected cattle. I urge the minister to see that there are enough veterinarians in those areas to ensure the efficient inspection of cattle, so we can prevent these serious situations from arising.
Has the minister any idea how many veterinarians will be taken on from college this year?
I gave those figures at an earlier date and I do not happen to have them with me. They will be found in Hansard.
I hardly think the minister understands my question. I should like to know the number of new veterinarians that will be coming into the service upon graduation from college this spring.

I believe that information is on Hansard. My memory is that there are about five hundred in college at present. All of them will not graduate this spring, but those figures have all been given to the house. I can bring them down again if that is desired. I understand that the number in colleges now is considered by those who have knowledge of the situation to be sufficient to practically eliminate the shortage when they have completed their courses, but the shortage will continue for a few years, of course. There is nothing you or I can do about that.

There are over one hundred men graduating from the Ontario Veterinary

Supply-Agriculture
College this year. Has the minister no idea as to the number entering the service this spring?
I gave the number once and it appears in Hansard. I am not going to guess at it now.
What page of Hansard?

I could look it up, but you
have as much time as I have to do that.
How many areas have been taken on for the purpose of T.B. tests, and is it the purpose of the government to accept those new areas before the tests are completed in the areas already set up?

We are accepting areas, I would say continuously. An order goes out on an average of once every two weeks. It depends on the action taken in the counties. A vote is taken to determine whether or not they desire to make application and, where the circumstances surrounding the application meet the requirements of the act, we take them in. We accept them immediately they come along. That does not mean we go in and start checking them the next day. We may not have the veterinarians to do that, but as soon as veterinarians can be secured we go on with the work.

Can the minister say whether they have started to test any of those new areas they have accepted? Is it fair to start a test in the new areas when there are so many old areas which have lapsed after the government has spent considerable money in setting them up?

Sometimes it is a question. Take a county like the one that has been set up recently in Quebec, between the St. Lawrence river and the United States border. About the only natural market they have for their livestock is across into the United States since we have opened the United States boundary line. We naturally give some preference to areas such as that and carry on the investigations there at once. In other places where districts have extended and finally come close together, and where the people are in a county which is in between two counties which have already been done, they have considerable hardship in selling animals even across the road. In those instances we would attempt to go in to clean up that position, and thus get the whole area put into one solid block. We try to follow the different counties in the area in which they make application.

The minister may know the object of my question. For two or three years I have asked him when the department

was going to retest Durham county. When I last asked him the minister said that if I could find veterinarians to do it they would do it. I wonder whether he can give me any assurance that the test will be started there before long.
Have you found the veterinarians?

I do not think that is my
job?

Is any publicity being carried on through the department to speed up those areas so that we might wipe out T.B. in our province? I wish to point out to the minister and to the committee that since a number of my constituents have been taken seriously ill something should be done to wipe out T.B. in cattle.

We have been responsible for the policy being in existence at all. When I say "we" I mean the Department of Agriculture, which went into the areas many years before I had anything to do with it. It is the Department of Agriculture in Ottawa which sold the idea of inspecting areas for T.B., and we had great difficulty. For example, Alberta refused to come in at all or have any part of it until after I became minister. They eventually came in. On the other hand, the maritime provinces had their entire area covered by checks that had been made before I came into the department some fourteen years ago. In Saskatchewan we started at a later date; at about the time that Mr. Motherwell was Minister of Agriculture we started to line up districts, and the officials have been working in all parts of Canada since just prior to the war just as rapidly as we can find veterinarians to do the work. The house has never limited the amount; the government itself has never limited the amount. And when we found it possible to spend more than we have put in the estimates we have come to the house, as we are doing now, and asked for a supplementary vote in order to pay for it. It has not been limited except by the difficulty of finding veterinarians to do the work.
That of course is associated with the question asked by my hon. friend who wishes to know how many veterinarians there are in the colleges. There is a considerable number in the colleges and in their senior years they are being given work. They are being put out, along with fully qualified veterinarians, to cover these districts more rapidly than they would otherwise be covered. We employ all we can get during the summer months.
The minister did not quite answer my question. I think the minister will agree with me that in order

to have a vote which would conform with the setting up of these areas the people must understand the situation. That requires education. I am sure the minister will agree with me on that. It is not wholly a question of having veterinarians, although I know that is a real problem. I would urge the minister to speed up the education of our people so that they will see the need of this work.

I want to point out to the
minister that he must have misunderstood my question. A moment ago he made the statement that I had asked how many students there were in the colleges. I did not ask that.
The hon. member asked how many were coming out this spring, which is pretty much the same thing.
Taken on by the department this spring.

I want to make an observation. The minister knows that the incidence of hog cholera was very great in days gone by. I am speaking of a quarter of a century ago, before the department had such good control of hog feeding areas close to large centres of population. What was referred to as hog cholera was probably swine fever instead of cholera in the full sense of the term. It was a costly item, not so much for the department itself, because at that time their control was not as good as it is now. It was a costly item to those who were engaged in that particular line of work. I am thinking back, sir, to the days of the first war when at Camp Borden some bright minds thought that what was going to waste should be used in the production of more pork. I do not like to mention names of those who are dead and gone, but the tragedy of Colonel Low at Camp Borden cost the government perhaps $100,000. The difficulty was not only at Camp Borden but in a good many other military areas.
I congratulate the department through you, sir, on taking careful and definite control over the feeding of hogs from waste from hotels, military camps and what not. My purpose in rising now is to ask you to see to it that that is continued for the general economy of Canada. Having said that, I should like to put on record some of the difficulties which your department will find when it is administering this act. I do not refer to difficulties in administering the act but in the remedial ideas which might be inculcated in the minds of those who are feeding animals with this waste material which should be conserved.
I want to delay the committee a moment or two to recite one fact which might be for the general advantage of the whole industry in the days to come. If you listen to the radio every day you will hear soap operas urging
Supply-Agriculture
the people of Canada to use more and more soap of different kinds. Soap, an alkali product, finds its way into the kitchens where waste material is conserved to be sold to those who are feeding that material to produce more and more pork products. The net result of the whole equation is this. Twenty years ago sixty-four million pounds of soap were consumed in Canada. Today almost double that quantity is consumed, a great deal of it in the kitchens of the Chateau Laurier, thej restaurant in the parliament buildings and in other places. It is washed down and finds its way into the garbage can. From the garbage can it finds its way into the stomach of the hog. In the hog producing centres where hogs are fed garbage it sets up a fever. This is the fever which your department, Mr. Minister, sometimes calls hog cholera; and we are now asked to vote $100,000 to compensate for any losses which might be sustained in this connection.
However I would ask the minister's department to do some research work. If they did they would find a line of demarcation between swine fever, which arises from the feeding of garbage

from such places as our parliamentary restaurant here-and hog cholera which, I believe the minister will agree with me, is almost on a par with what is known south of the equator as foot and mouth disease.
I hope the minister's department will spend some of this money to guide and direct those who are operating establishments of the kind I have mentioned, which produce hundreds of thousands of pounds of pork products for the general advantage of. Canada. Those instructions would act as a guide in the matter of feeding, and not only by way of taking bacteriological data. I have in mind the position taken by officers of the department, that once the product is boiled and steamed, that is sufficient procedure to take before feeding. I would ask the department to go a little further and determine the alkalinity of the resultant food product collected from restaurants in the urban centres. The department should seek to find some method of neutralizing that alkalinity which, to my mind and the minds of many others who have had some experience in this matter, sets up this so-called swine fever. This disease proves itself devastating to the interests of farmers who make their living from the feeding of hogs. I would ask the department to see if it cannot find some method of controlling these large feeding establishments -and when I use the word "large" I am asking hon. members through you, Mr. Chairman, to listen to the voice of experience; because it is only twenty-eight years ago that I left the feeding of animals, found myself

Supply-Agriculture
leasing my premises and coming here to accept the great and high privilege of sitting in this community; perhaps I should say this communion.
If I may, by way of an aside I would say that sometimes I think I made a mistake when I left the pigs and came into politics. Perhaps I would have been far better off had I stayed with the pigs. It may be that I should write a book which, after three decades, is something one should be allowed to do.
Returning to my original theme, and speaking seriously for the general advantage of the industry in Canada, I do hope that through you, Mr. Chairman, I may ask the minister to take some portion of this $100,000, a vote with which I am heartily in accord, and see if further developments cannot be made in the research which has been under way for the last quarter century, so that the innocent, ordinary farmer's son who goes into this line of business-and by the way, a very profitable line of business-may be guided in the feeding of these waste products and turning them into real money. I should hope that some portion of this vote might be used for research work along the lines I have indicated. I trust I have made myself clear to the minister. If I have not I should be only too happy to answer one or two questions, only to be sure that he understands what I have been saying.
To speak briefly, hog cholera is not like the foot and mouth disease. It is foreign to this country. But the lesser form of swine fever, caused by excessive alkali found in the soaps which find their way into the garbage cans-* soaps which are excessively and unnecessarily advertised in soap operas-is a curse to the hog-feeding trade which uses garbage as a feeding base.

May I say, with regard to what has been said, that it would be impossible for me to say that part of this item would be taken. What the hon. member has said refers to the preceding item, the vote of $54,000 which deals with the administration of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act and the Meat and Canned Foods Act. That deals with the general operation of the branch of the department to which the hon. member has referred.
I shall see that the hon. member's remarks are brought to the attention of the officials. I am sure they will be fully aware of the importance of what he has said. But in case they are not, I shall bring them to their attention.
I thank the minister; I shall add what I have said to the $54,000 question.

May I make a suggestion to the minister which I believe to be worthy of consideration. In the west we have what is known as Bang's disease or contagious abortion in many herds. I understand that in humans it is called undulant fever. Many head of stock are lost through this disease.
May I suggest to the minister that where through the Animal Contagious Diseases Act it is possible to take care of tuberculosis, the prevention of Bang's disease should also be considered and, if possible, should come under the same administration.

Item agreed to.
Marketing service-
571.	Subsidies for cold storage warehouses under the Cold Storage Act, and grants, in the amounts detailed in the estimates-further amount required, $75,335.

I would like to draw one matter to the minister's attention. While I do not think there has been a change in the law in this respect, I believe there was a change in its administration last year, which may be reflected to some extent in the figures we have before us. In cold storage construction, because of fair wages legislation it was necessary to have the approval of the Department of Labour of wages which were fixed. Heretofore there has been a clause in contracts stating that the individual or firm building a cold storage plant would comply with the provisions of the act.
Last year, the year for which this money is voted, the contract was changed. Instead of having a general clause, a schedule was set out in the contract enumerating the wages to be paid. At least in one particular instance of which I have knowledge, those wages were based upon the scale obtaining in an urban centre many miles away. Those wage rates, of course, were subject to union negotiations and other matters of the kind. Undoubtedly the wages in those urban areas would have been considered fair and reasonable. But the rate set forth in the contract of which I am speaking was much higher than that then prevailing in the rural area in which the cold storage plant was being built. There were further supplementary provisions stating that overtime should be paid for anything over eight hours, that there should be a five-day week and other conditions.
The whole contract was changed, in so far as that clause was concerned, with the net result that the subsidy payable under this vote was thereby increased by the additional cost. What is more important, the scale of wages in the rural community in question is entirely dislocated, with the result that farmers and other persons employing help are threatened with an attempted migration

toward the one contractor or organization engaged in the construction of the cold storage plant. It would appear to me that the section in the original contract is preferable. I am wondering why the change was made and if the minister could see that some consideration is given to this matter so that we can avoid having rules that are absolutely inapplicable to the conditions prevailing.

The honey producer co-operatives in a number of provinces have reported that there is quite a surplus of honey at the present time. I was wondering whether the Department of Agriculture and the various honey producer co-operatives could not get in touch with the Canadian Commercial Corporation with a view to having them seek markets for this surplus. I recall that a few days ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that in some instances the Canadian Commercial Corporation assisted private industries in getting markets for their products. There is no question that if that could be done the honey producers of Canada would be much indebted.
The minister has not answered the question asked by the hon. member.

I listened to what the hon. member had to say and I notice that there is an item for one plant in Nova Scotia. I do not know whether that is the one that he was referring to. The item for canning, United Fruit Companies of Nova Scotia Limited, is for $19,988 and I presume that is the item that has been spoken to. I shall look into all the features that have been mentioned by the hon. member and see to it that if any mistakes have been made we do not repeat them.

I was not wondering about the minister answering my question now because we will have an opportunity later on when we can deal more effectively with this matter. When the general estimates are before us I should like the minister to provide us with a copy of the specifications now required for the construction of these plants. I am sure that they would be of interest to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply in view of the great shortage of building materials.
I believe the minister will find that a change was made in the specifications after a change had been made in the personnel of the department. As a result of those changes, instead of having one thickness of sheeting, a double thickness was required which entails a considerable expense and an extra use of material which apparently was in short supply. I presume that these specifications vary in the different parts of the country depending upon the geographical location.
Supply-Agriculture
I shall have all the details here when the general estimates are before the committee.
Does this subsidy include anything for the maintenance or running charges of cold storage warehouses?

It is to cover only the capital cost. When a co-operative or private individual or corporation proposes to build a cold storage plant which the public may utilize, if application is made to the government before operations are commenced the government may pay thirty per cent of the cost. Half is paid in the first year and the rest is spread over the next four years. This v/ould not apply only to the parts of the premises that are used for cold storage; it would apply to that part used by management for the operation of the plant. But if a creamery or some other business is carried on in the same building a clear division is made as between that part and the part utilized for cold storage.

Do I understand that the conversion of a common storage into cold storage would not warrant a subsidy? In Summer-land they are converting a common storage into a cold storage and they want to know whether they can get the subsidy.

Each case is considered on its merits. The regulations are that application must be made to the government before any work is done or before any contract is let. The first act is to make application. If a plant is already being used for some other purpose, or if an addition is going to be made, consideration would have to be given to that particular case. There might be some difficulty in the case of a conversion from common to cold storage. I would want to have a check made of the case before saying it could or could not be done.
An application is now in.
Has it been dealt with?
No.
It will be dealt with on the basis I have set out.

Item agreed to.
Special-
572.	To provide assistance for the replacement of maple production equipment-further amount required. $61,729.

There are no details for this item and the next two following items, which together total $1,486,729. Perhaps the minister could make a statement with regard to these items.

Supply-A griculture

I think I can explain the whole three. The first item is to provide assistance for the replacement of maple production equipment, and the amount asked for is $61,729. The origin of this vote is this: Back about 1936 the United States raised an objection to syrup from the province of Quebec on the ground that it contained lead poison. The syrup complained about was analysed and it was found that the complaint was justified. The syrup which had been condemned for human consumption was utilized in the manufacture of cigarette tobacco so we did not lose the sale. However, we gave an undertaking that we would co-operate with the province of Quebec and the maple syrup producers to eliminate this trouble.
Some person had made buckets which would not rust by putting a lead coating on them. After the sap had been in the pail some chemical action took place which absorbed some of the ingredients of the lead into the syrup and produced lead poison. We undertook, in co-operation with the provincial government and the owners of the bucket, to pay one-third of the cost of removing this equipment. This has been progressing year after year. The reason for this supplementary amount is that they took out of operation equipment to the value of $61,729 over and above the vote of last year. We are simply asking that that be voted in order that payments can be made under our agreement to pay one-third.
This applies only to the province of Quebec?
Yes.
There was $300,000 in the estimates last year. Does this vote mean that a total of $361,729 is being expended just for buckets?

It is not only buckets; it is the vats that are used for boiling down the syrup. All this equipment is of a similar type. A total of $300,000 has been spent every year since the year I spoke of, or up until the war began. During the war it was cut down, not because we stopped it, but because they could not get the substitutes for the equipment. Since the end of the war it has been $300,000, and we are stepping it up in order to get rid of this payment as rapidly as possible.
For how many more years do you expect to have to pay it?
I am not certain, but I hope it will not be very many more.
Was any definite estimate made when the agreement was entered into?

No. There was an amount, which is not in my mind at the moment-it is too long ago-that the equipment was valued at. I believe it was thought at that time that it would take about five or six years, but as I stated a moment ago the war came on in about the middle of that period. When the war was over we decided to try to get rid of this as rapidly as we could. We have not been holding the expenditure down; we have been saying, "go ahead and clean it up as fast as you can and we will meet the payments." The operators in connection with that are the provincial government, not we. Whatever they bill us for we pay.
Can you tell us the number of persons who are benefiting under this vote?
Oh, most of the producers of syrup in the province of Quebec. I cannot give you the exact number offhand, but it is nearly all of them.
Had they all purchased this equipment?

Most of them. I think my hon. friend will agree with me that there was a time when all the buckets we had in the province of Ontario were so rusty that you wondered whether or not you could put them up. Naturally when someone came around with a type of bucket that was not going to rust at all, and was going to look very nice, everybody would buy it provided the price was not too high. Apparently they had a good salesman, and they sold this kind of equipment to nearly everybody. Probably we would never have discovered anything particularly wrong with it if it had not been that we were exporting syrup. I think we ran into difficulties because the Americans were running into the same difficulties with the same kind of equipment on the other side of the line, and therefore they checked on ours and brought up the same question.
Was none of this equipment sold in Ontario at all?
If there was we would be prepared to take care of it in the same way, but no Ontario government has brought it to our attention so far.

I understand from the minister's remarks that the administration is under the provincial governments, and that the federal government pays out this amount to assist in removing these poor containers in order to protect the health of the people. In driving through some parts of the province of Ontario I have noticed some very rusty looking buckets. I suppose that they are some that have not yet been taken in.
No, the rusty ones apparently were all right; it was the ones that would not rust.

They were still in use. I take it that the department intends to renew all buckets. At any rate, I should like to know what administration you have to see that all of these faulty buckets are taken in and destroyed so that they cannot be used any more.

That is carried on by the province, but of course it is checked by our officials before we make payment. If you had had the experience that some of us have had in getting payments passed by treasury board, you would realize that they do not pay anything unless they are absolutely convinced that it ought to be paid for what has been done. In other words, a very complete check is made. The provincial government see that it is all paid, and then they bill us for one-third of it. The farmer pays one-third, the province pays one-third and we pay one-third, but we are absolutely satisfied that the buckets have been replaced before we pay anything. As a matter of fact, new ones have been bought, and that is what we pay for.
Can the minister say what the cost is of the total replacements up to date?

Speaking from memory- and I would not want to be held too closely to this-I think that the vote for the three years prior to the war was $300,000 each year, and I think most of it was spent each year. After the war we started off with the same amount, $300,000, and we have been working on it now for either two or three years. This year they have spent $61,729 more than the $300,000.
I think this whole discussion should have been held in camera, because we are just beginning to find out now that since 1937 we have been using maple syrup that has contained lead poison.
It never was held in camera. It has been up here so many times that I know the story quite well.

Item agreed to.
573.	To provide for assistance to the province of Nova Scotia in the removal of aged maple trees and of least desirable varieties in Nova Scotia under such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council-further amount required, $1,000,000.

Explanations have been made by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture which started the discussion about the impossibility of estimating exactly, and at the end of the year 29087-142J
Supply-Agriculture
there has to be a little juggling back and forth to get the books cleaned up. That explanation may apply to most of the items, but it certainly does not apply to this item. In this case the amount that was voted last year was $500,000. That was spent, and in addition another $1 million was spent. In other words, there was three times as much spent as was voted. Therefore any explanation, such as the one already given by the two ministers, certainly does not apply to this item.
As a matter of fact, it seems to me to illustrate clearly that this government pays very little attention to the money which is voted by parliament, or whether money is voted by parliament at all. They just proceed to spend it and then try to find an explanation for it afterward.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This has not been spent yet.
A lot of it has.

The Minister of Agriculture gave an explanation in an interjection in the budget debate. He said that the government had been authorized to uproot 240,000 trees, and that the program was to cover three years, but they had found that the whole thing could be done in the one year. Therefore they spent the whole $1,500,000 which ordinarily would have been spread over three years. As a matter of fact, it seems to me that this $1 million is to a very large extent that direct beneficence which the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply spoke about as having been extended to Digby-Annapolis-Kings during the by-election, and it is a part of the same money that the Minister of Finance mentioned when he wrote a letter to these people. Before the item is passed, I think we certainly should have a much better explanation than we have had up to date.

As my hon. friend says, I gave a short explanation of this in the budget debate. I am rather amused at the remarks of the hon. member for Regina City. I do not think there is anyone in the house who has been more insistent about getting money spent for certain purposes, and having announcements made with regard to the spending of money that has never been voted by this house, than the hon. member for Regina City.
Assiniboia.

No, my friend, the hon. member for Regina City was making some remarks a few moments ago. With regard to this particular item, it really had nothing to do with the by-election in Digby-Annapolis-Kings. I think my hon. friends will understand that before I am through. I have never

Supply-Agriculture
heard any less proper criticism than that which has been made of the statement made some time ago by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, in commenting upon certain things which were being discussed at the time, made some reference to the amount of money which had been spent in the constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings.
It is foolish to think that the money spent, to which the hon. member was referring, had anything to do with the by-election. The expenditure started back in 1939, and has amounted to between $1,500,000 and $3 million a year ever since. It had nothing to do with any general election or by-election; it had to do with the fact that before the war the Annapolis valley was selling eighty per cent of its apples to Great Britain. The day the war started, or within a very few days afterward, Great Britain said they were not going to buy any apples in the first year of the war, and that was the fact with which we were confronted, as were the people of the province of Nova Scotia. Eighty per cent of their market was completely gone, so they came here and asked for some consideration of their position; and it was agreed that any industry, particularly any part of the industry of agriculture, that was subject to difficulties of that kind arising purely from the war should be given some consideration.
As I said a moment ago, from that time down to the present the matter has been considered every year; and in spite of the fact that we lost the Digby-Annapolis-Kings by-election, in spite of the fact that my friend represents the constituency now and sits on the other side of the house, we are giving the matter exactly the same consideration this year that we gave it any other year. The delegation is in Ottawa now, for the third time. That is the same number of times they have been here every year since 1939. I am not in a position to say this afternoon what we are going to do for them, but in the light of what we have done in the past I know we are going to do something this year, because they are still in difficulties.
So are you.

Well, if we are it is not because of anything having to do with this. More than a year ago, before there was any talk at all about a by-election in Nova Scotia, two or three members of the government of that province and a very strong delegation, including C.C.F.'ers, Conservatives and Liberals, came here and submitted to the government the position in which they found themselves. They said they should not go on indefinitely spending the money they were putting up themselves and the money we

were spending and the losses some other people were taking, and they proposed a plan under which they would pull out a certain number of trees over a three-year period, if we would finance that undertaking. At the same time they proposed that the provincial government would finance the grafting of other trees-and there was no political graft in that job, which was not done by our government. They simply said that one job was the pulling out of trees and the planting of others. Another job was cutting the limbs off some of the trees and grafting new varieties on them. The grafting is a bigger and more expensive job per tree than the other, but it gets production at an earlier date, since it does not take so long for a tree to produce when it is treated in this way as it does if you pull out one tree and put in another one. The province undertook to finance the grafting job, and suggested that we finance the pulling out of the trees; and it was suggested that we should take out a number of trees each year until markets were found for the remaining varieties of apples, when it would be possible to cut down on the other payments.
So we started on that job. No one anticipated that it would be found possible to pull out these trees as rapidly as it was done; but they pulled the full number, completing then-work early in the season before there was any by-election at all called in the valley. The hon. member will know more about that than I do. I believe the number of trees intended to be dealt with in the first year was exceeded in a very short period of time. Then they came back to us and said, "You agreed to pull 240,000 trees. We can pull 300,000 trees this year. Let us get this job over with, and that will make it possible to consider a reduction at an earlier date than otherwise would be possible of the costs down in that area to the federal government". The provincial government asked us to consider allowing them to go ahead. The provincial government actually arranged for the pulling of the trees and billed us with the cost. So we said "All right; go ahead and carry out your three-year contract", which was 240,000 trees, and they did that just as rapidly as they had been proceeding with what was provided for in the first year of the contract.
I repeat, and emphasize, that we had nothing whatever to do with the speed at which they were proceeding. The work was being carried out by the people in Nova Scotia, not by us. After they had pulled their full number of trees contracted for in the first year they simply came back and said, "Can we go on and pull the remainder"? I submitted the question to council, and after the Department of Finance had looked into the

matter they agreed that in the long run it would probably pay us better to have these trees pulled as rapidly as possible than to stretch it out and have to take care of the apples grown on those trees from year to year, for which there was no market. We have been buying those apples, putting them in cans, or having them dehydrated and then at the end of the season giving some of them away, after incurring a great deal of expense. The decision was that it would be better to have these trees pulled out as rapidly as possible. We told them to go ahead and pull the full number required under the agreement.
That agreement, by the way, had been previously submitted to this house and passed upon. Last year the house voted an amount sufficient to cover the cost for the first year, and in doing so endorsed the contract for the whole three years. The only criticism that might be made is that when this work was completed, which was after the election was over, they said they could still go on and pull another sixty thousand trees, and we told them to go ahead. So, instead of costing us $500,000 the whole thing cost $1,500,000, and this vote covers the extra million.
It is all very well to make these slighting, offhand remarks about by-elections and so on, but I think my hon. friend opposite, the member elected, would be the first to admit the truth of everything I have said, namely that in the first instance the contract had nothing to do with any by-election or general election; in the second place that it was the right thing to do, because in this way we cut down the amount we are going to have to put up from year to year from now on in supporting the marketing of the surplus apples of the province of Nova Scotia. There is the further fact that we went ahead and assumed obligations after the by-election was all over, which is a clear indication that this had nothing whatever to do with any byelection and was not a handout to anyone in order to get votes. If we in this house are going to expect things to be done by any government, I do not care whether it be this government or a future government that is appealed to, every time someone proposes an expenditure in some part of the country, those coming from that area cannot be saying the only thing he has in mind is the next election. If that kind of argument is going to be utilized, then we are going to be in difficulty all the time. It will be difficult to get the money to start with, and it will certainly be difficult to carry on. There was never any thought of a by-election or anything having to do with a by-election in connection with this particular expenditure. I repeat that I think the member from that constituency will be the first to agree with me.
