speechtext: As I said the other day, one should not attempt to be humorous in a letter.
As I said, if the minister is in trouble-

I am not in any trouble.

Supply-Agriculture
It is very nice of him to suggest he is not, but I think he is. However, he need not blame the members on this side of the house for that, he should blame his colleagues.

I am glad this matter has come up. I was not in the house when this press report first came to the attention of the house. I wrote a letter to my very good friend the secretary of the apple growers association, and I said I was gratified at the expression of appreciation. Then, I added a sentence in a semi-humorous vein, "I am sorry that the appreciation did not take the form of more votes in the by-election," and I put a couple of exclamation marks after that sentence. Those exclamation marks did not appear in the press report, of course. As I said, it only proves that one should not try to be humorous in a letter.

Before this item carries, and since I am being put more or less in the position of the nut in the nutcracker, I should like to say a word or two. I do not want to be caught up in any argument about the beneficences or otherwise of this government. As a matter of fact, I never did see the letter to which reference has been made, although I have some slight knowledge of its background. I think the minister certainly will not question the references which have been made in the press. I do know there was a personal relationship between himself and the person to whom the letter was written.
I want to say that in general I agree entirely with what the Minister of Agriculture has said with respect to this vote. It is true that the matter was started many years ago. It is true that this government has carried on this policy, and although a change in its administration was made a year ago when the provincial government was brought in, it is something that existed long before the by-election. Certainly, appropriations were made prior to the election. I am not saying that more favourable consideration may not have been given because of the by-election, because of course I was not in a position to know of those matters. Certainly, so far as it was concerned, there was no question of political implication at the time the appropriation was made. No one had any control over that, least of all the Minister of Agriculture.
The Liberal party in its advertising throughout the campaign used language which was even more extreme than that which may have been jocularly used by the Minister of Finance in portraying the beneficence of this government to the constituents of Digby-Annapolis-Kings. Certainly, every effort was made so that those people would

not feel like voting for any other party at that time.
In view of the many remarks that have been made, I think I should say that the moneys have been properly spent. Undoubtedly, in the expenditure of government funds, criticism can be made of certain minor details. These would be of a minor nature and do not reflect on the expenditure of this money as a whole.
I am happy to know that negotiations are being concluded, and that the minister is prepared to finalize those on a basis similar to the ones which he has concluded in the past few years. I may say that is a happy announcement to the people of the Annapolis valley.
Can the minister tell us how many people have received a share of this money?
I believe all the growers in the valley. There has been a difference of opinion as to how many there are. I have been saying there are about 4,500, but some people tell me there are not that many.
The cheques must have been sent out and there must be a record of them.

The money is paid to the provincial governments and the cheques go out from them.

Progress reported.

I should not think it would be necessary for anyone to rise because I am sure the hon. member for Halifax is most anxious to give an explanation of the bill he is sponsoring. I hope he will not be denied that opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 80, which was letter M of the Senate, is a simple bill intended to make three changes in the internal organization of the company respecting the board of directors and the date of the annual meeting.
The Dominion Atlantic Railway Company was incorporated by act of this parliament in 1895, and pursuant to section 6 (c) of the Railway Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 170, it has been named a work for the general advantage of Canada. sor, Kentville, Annapolis Royal and Digby with a terminus in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia.

maintopic: THE SISTERS OF SAINT ELIZABETH HOSPITAL
THE SISTERS OF SAINT ELIZABETH HOSPITAL
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 125 (from the Senate) to incorporate the Sisters of Saint Elizabeth Hospital.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the Sisters of Saint Elizabeth are an order of nursing sisters and this bill is to meet their request for incorporation under the laws of Canada. As their mother house and main hospital are in the constituency which I have the honour to

represent, I feel that I am indeed privileged to have the honour to sponsor this bill.
May I, at this time, pay a tribute to all those in the nursing profession-be they lay people or members of religious orders. These people make possible the operation of our hospitals in all parts of our country. They are, so to speak, the Marthas of our health services.
From the pioneer days of our Humboldt district in 1903, up to 1912, we did not have the benefit of a hospital, the nearest being over eighty miles away, with only prairie trails for roads. With the means of transportation of that time, a trip of that length was difficult for a person in good health; but when it came to taking our sick and injured to hospital, few people nowadays can imagine the additional suffering caused to the patient and the anxiety of the family.
In 1912 a small group of nursing sisters who had come from Hungary opened a small hospital in the town of Humboldt. By good management on the part of the sisters, and the generosity of the people of that district, two large additions have been added to the original building and, as years went by, up-to-date and modern equipment has been installed, so that now the care and services rendered in this hospital compare very favourably with the larger hospitals in the cities.
While the members of this order of nursing sisters belong to the Roman Catholic church, people of all religious denominations in the entire district that it serves feel that it is a community undertaking for the benefit of all.
Very often a member of the United Church and at other times a member of the Anglican Church was president of the hospital ladies aid. A few years ago there was urgent need to have a new heating plant and laundry built, and a member of the Jewish faith headed the finance committee in the appeal for funds. In my opinion our hospital has played its full part in furthering a spirit of good will and co-operation among all the people, in addition to taking care of our sick and injured.
As the years went by, following urgent requests from people of other districts, they opened hospitals at Cudworth and Macklin, Saskatchewan, which brought to those districts the same benefits and services that we experience in ours.
In 1915, the sisters in charge obtained incorporation under the laws of the province of Saskatchewan, and in view of the fact that requests have come from beyond the province for extension of their services to other parts, they would now like the wider charter that this bill would provide.
I will not take the time of the house to go into any of the details concerning the finan-

cial affairs and other matters in which some members may be interested; but if this is referred to the committee on private bills, I shall be more than pleased to give any member the fullest possible information. In the meantime, may I solicit the unanimous support of hon. members of the house for this bill.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I scarcely need to stress the importance of the bill of which I now move second reading. I have already done so. In the past objection was raised to my bill on the grounds that it would hamper freedom of speech and would inevitably favour undercover communistic activity. One thing is certain. Should my bill become law, communistic propaganda would be paralysed to a large extent in Canada, because communists would be unable to use the mail or to address the public as a means of propagating their ideology. As for their underground activities, that concerns the R.C.M.P. Last year, it was contended that the approval of my bill would favour, in communist dominated countries, propaganda against freedom of speech within their own boundaries. In my opinion, the trial of His Eminence Cardinal Mindszenty, Hungarian primate, is a stinging rebuttal to those who believe that freedom of opinion still exists in Russia or in countries under its domination. May I be permitted, in that connection, to quote President Truman, as follows:
The conviction of the Hungarian prelate is the infamous act of a kangaroo court.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in every country where communists have managed to penetrate, they have always done so with the help of freedom of speech which is, and rightly, the stamp of democracy. However, no sooner had they gained power in the countries they now control than the very freedom of speech they had used as a means to an end immediately vanished.
Communists are against every form of religion and in order to destroy them in our own country they do not hesitate to use every medium of propaganda at their disposal. In this, I agree with His Eminence Cardinal Spellman. I believe it is high time to deprive them of their means of propaganda.
It should be remembered that we are Christians and that every day the house opens its sittings with the following prayer:
That peace and happiness, truth and justice, religion and piety, may be established among us for all generations. These, and all other necessaries for them and for us, we humbly beg in the name and through the mediation of Jesus Christ, our most blessed Lord and Saviour.

Criminal Code
Hon. members know tnat only one hour is set aside at stated intervals to allow for a vote on this bill. May I, therefore, once again, as I have done in the past, request hon. members to stop their filibustering which, though seemingly in support of the bill, only serves to prevent the question from being put during the hour set aside for this purpose by the rules of the house.
If some clause of the bill does not suit them, they need only object when it is considered in committee. Moreover, I would advise these hon. gentlemen that every year, as long as I am a member of this house, I shall introduce this bill which I deem essential to any democracy concerned with protecting itself.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to oppose this measure and in doing so I hope my hon. friend will not characterize my effort as a filibuster. May I say to him that if he brings in a bill like this every year as he just said he would, if I am in the house with him I shall oppose it every year without thinking anything whatsoever about filibustering. The hon. member made reference to the importance of the measure. I am beginning to fear that it has an importance which he has failed so far to sense.
Not only would this bill get rid of the communist propaganda to which the hon. member objects; it might eventually get rid of nearly everybody in this house. I do not know whether my hon. friend has noticed that he makes no attempt to define in his measure just what communism means. He wants to rule out communism or the communist party, he wants to deprive them of the rights of citizenship which every Canadian citizen should enjoy, but he also extends the provisions of his bill to those who hold similar ideas. I have heard hon. members in this house charge nearly everybody with having those ideas. Certainly they have been imputed often to the group to which I belong. I have heard hon. members actually charge the government with having socialistic and communistic ideas. I notice that some of the most prominent citizens of Canada have been charged with that sort of thing. In fact it was not long since that I heard that Premier Manning was charged with that by some recalcitrants.
If we are going to have a law as rigid as this it should define exactly the type of crime that is going to be charged against those who are supposed to be in violation of it. I believe the people of Canada have been asking for a bill of rights and I think they should have a bill of rights. So far no bill of rights has made its appearance, but here we have a bill of wrongs that we are asked to support in the name of all that is best in

this country, in the name of Christianity, in the name of liberty and so forth.
Yet in the very name of those great and sacred things I am asking this house to reject it. It is neither Christian nor democratic nor has it that sense of liberty which we so much prize, at least in words if not in deeds. I would say that this is merely a reflex of, or perhaps it is symptomatic of, a reactionary hysteria which threatens to overwhelm sane judgment and sweep it from that position of predominance which properly it should hold in the affairs of state. No matter how dangerous communist philosophy and practice may be, we must not be so panic-stricken that we adopt their methods against ourselves before they have a chance to do so. In reality that is what we are doing by this bill. The tendency is not confined to this bill. We have seen tendencies in other respects throughout the country generally. We have seen certain religious groups subjected to treatment which was far from being democratic. We have seen touches of racial discrimination. We have seen legislation granted to prohibit the organization of labour, and we have seen a tendency not long ago in this very city to stand in the way of freedom of speech.
I point out to the house that the bill now before us is nothing more or less than the restoration of that pernicious principle which was in section 98 of the criminal code, and which was removed some years ago after many discussions had taken place in the house with respect thereto. Section 98 of the criminal code was conceived in hysteria and born in iniquity. During its life it disgraced the name of freedom and democracy. It was passed in 1919, and the late Mr. Woodsworth, who used to lead the group to which I belong, was a victim of that same measure. He spent a good deal of his time in the house trying to remove it, not because he had been a victim of it, but because he loved liberty and knew that such legislation was the very reverse of the principle of liberty. It was repealed in 1936. That legislation had pretty much the same effect that this bill would have. Under that legislation bibles that were printed in other languages were confiscated by policemen because they did not understand the languages in which they were written, and thought that they might be subversive.
I should like to refer my hon. friend to something said by the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe, one of the great statesmen from Quebec, who sat in this house with great honour to himself and to the people who elected him, and who performed great services for the nation. In speaking against a measure that in spirit is precisely the same

as the measure that my hon. friend is now sponsoring, Mr. Lapointe had this to say, after having been reminded that bibles in the English language were confiscated as well as bibles in foreign languages, and I refer to page 3899 of Hansard of June 19, 1936. Mr. Lapointe said:
I did not know that, but it makes the matter so much worse.
Do you not think conditions have changed?

I continue to read:
A man was arrested because he had in his possession a copy of Plato's Republic. In the United States, under a similar provision, a man was arrested because he had in his possession some literature that happened to have been written by Thomas Jefferson, who was one of the authors of the Declaration of Independence and later president of the United States. When the man told that to the officer who arrested him, the officer replied, "Well, we will take care of you now and we will get that man Jefferson afterwards."
That is just an idea of the absurdity you can expect from ill-conceived legislation such as we have here. I think the people of Canada will credit the removal of that nefarious measure, section 98, from the statute books of Canada to the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe.
For the edification of my hon. friend opposite, let me quote some further utterances of his distinguished compatriot on a measure exactly the same as this. He said:
I have said that war regulations should not be converted into peace statutes.

Conditions have changed
since that time.

The principle of liberty does not change. The fears of people change, and sometimes people who are nervous become so afraid of nothing that they run from shadows. Sometimes the thing they fear most is liberty itself, although they do not quite realize that is so. I continue with the quotation:
The order in council which I have quoted shows that the liberties of the citizens were infringed. In time of war this has to be done, but to do it in time of peace is a precedent which should not be created. Liberty is like air; we appreciate its values more when we are deprived of it. To govern is to foresee. After all it is possible that there may come a government with views and ideals different from those entertained by hon. members opposite and myself, and they could use the precedent so created to prevent the freedom of the people in other directions.
He goes on to say:
Benjamin Franklin said once, and I agree with this idea, that those who are ready to sacrifice liberty for the purpose of achieving some temporary safety deserve neither liberty nor safety. British justice, which holds every man innocent until he is proved guilty, is the surest safeguard against excesses, whether coming from communists or fascists, or an
Criminal Code
arbitrary dictatorship, from the left or from the right. We submit this legislation, not because we sympathize with revolutionaires but because we love and desire to protect the law-abiding and truthseeking citizens of this country.
I quote those words tonight, not only because they are apropos, but because they carry down through the years that fine, broad, vigorous spirit of democracy so characteristic of their author.
May I say to my hon. friend that I hope he appreciates how different his position is in his present role as sponsor of this measure to the part played by his distinguished compatriot whose words I have quoted, and who was instrumental in removing from the statute books of Canada vicious legislation similar to the statute now proposed by my hon. friend. I can assure my hon. friend, who is the sponsor of this bill, that he will bring no honour to himself, to this parliament or to his nation, nor will anything he has said in support of the measure be quoted by anyone in years to come except as proof of a lingering tendency toward fascism.
There might be a good excuse for legislation of this kind if we were not already sufficiently protected against anyone who might desire to upset our government, or by violence seek to usurp power. Again in this connection I must turn to one of our best authorities, the same right hon. gentleman I have been quoting. I refer my hon. friend to Hansard for 1936, volume 4, at page 3899, where the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe said:
There Is no sense of proportion in an enactment of this kind.
That also applies to this bill.
I showed that provision to an eminent professor of law at the university of Paris only two months ago. He said to me, "This is a blot on the statutes of any land," and it is. We have said that we must protect ourselves against disorderly elements. I repeat what I have said many times before. We have in the criminal code, which is based on the common law of England, all the provisions which make English law and British justice sufficient to meet all emergencies. The common law relating to sedition is already in our criminal code and always has been.
But communistic ideology was not spreading at that time.

Then Mr. Lapointe went on to quote sections 133 and 134 of the criminal code, and to give further proof that now, without further legislation of this kind, we are amply protected against any danger of the sort my hon. friend seems to fear. So the bill adds nothing to our legal protection, but it does deprive Canadian citizens of their liberties. In this connection I want to quote something said by Mr. Woodsworth in 1933. Referring to men who had been imprisoned
225S

Criminal Code
under section 98 he said, at page 2096 of
Hansard:
I should like to point out that these men did not commit any overt act whatever. They were not convicted of urging the use of force, nor were they convicted of using force. They were convicted of belonging to an association which was said to be affiliated with a body in Russia which did believe in the use of force; on that type of evidence they were convicted . . .
They were convicted for holding a certain belief, and I say that is something quite new in British law.
I point out that they would not need to commit an overt act under the legislation now proposed. So in this bill we are to be subjected to a penalty for having an idea; if you happen to have one that somebody thinks is wrong you may have to pay $5,000 or go to jail for twenty years. About the only person who would be safe under such a measure is a person who never had and never expected to have an idea; and I sincerely hope my hon. friend will some time have an idea and therefore qualify to come under the legislation he is now proposing. Then in 1922, at page 1390 of Hansard, Mr. Woodsworth had this to say, in connection with the same type of legislation:
I would suggest that we should be in keeping with the very best British practice if we condemned men only when they committed some overt act and not for merely thinking this or the other thing. In Japan, I believe, there is now a law against dangerous thoughts, and we seem to be approaching very near to the autocratic imperialism of Japan when we undertake to decide whether or not a man harbours dangerous ideas.
It is conceivable that a measure of this kind might pass the house if it were not considered. I recall that last year my hon. friend who is sponsoring this legislation wanted the bill passed before it was explained and discussed. As I say, if that had happened it might have passed; but it is not likely that such a bill could possibly pass this parliament. I doubt whether any hon. member has failed to grasp its implications, because by our training and traditions we hold the conviction that the right of a person to think, the right of a person to organize his fellows in support of an idea, the right of a citizen to speak or write in support of an idea, are liberties of which as a democracy we boast, and which we will not yield. Indeed, these very liberties are held up in contrast to Russia and Russian methods. If this legislation were to pass we should be bringing into practice, by deliberate act of parliament, those features of communism which we say we fear most. It is said that the communists suppress their opponents by force, and that they gain control of countries by force.
It is true, too.

I am not doubting it. These are the chief arguments against communism in this country. In this country many perhaps would have been following the communists if it had not been for the very fact that they use force, and the people of this country say, "We do not need to use force. We can get anything the people of this country want by the ballot; therefore we do not use force." But if you take that right away from them; if you say they must not express their opinions, they must not write articles, they must not propagandize their ideas, they must not be allowed to run for parliament, they must not be allowed to sit in parliament: then you say to them that the only way they can ever come to power in this country is not by the ballot but by force. Thus you say to all the people of Canada, "If the things the communists advocate are good, you cannot get them by the ballot; you must get them by force." So the difficulty is removed and they say, "All right; if that is the only way we can get what we want, then we will join." So you are doing a very dangerous thing if you give them that great lever, which most decidedly you will be placing in their hands if you take from them the right which we all enjoy to propagate whatever idea we may have and leave it to the people themselves, by their ballot, to decide what it is they want. If we adopt the methods of the communists and eliminate our opponents, then we are on a level with communism in the worst and most objectionable features of its philosophy.
If a bill similar to this were adopted in Russia we would be speaking against it, holding it up as an example of the worst kind of dictatorship and the smothering of liberty. Presumably if this bill were to pass, the communists in Russia would be pleased indeed, because it would be an acknowledgment that the parliament of Canada had adopted the tactics of communism, finding that the only way to keep peace.
The comparison is far-fetched.
The argument is absolutely logical and sound, and the definite outcome of the kind of legislation proposed here.

It does not
stand up.
Your bill is so loosely worded it could mean anything.
The bill could be amended.
I know of no way of amending a rotten egg, and this bill is just that.
Speaking of communism?
No. I am not speaking of communism, but I am trying to protect us from communistic methods.
You are scoring a great victory for them.
Your bill would be a greater victory for them.
No.

A much greater victory for them; that is the reason why I am opposing it. People will naturally say, if we pass legislation of this kind, "Since we have accepted the worst in communism, why not accept the best of it?"
The outlawing of a movement which is alleged to achieve its purposes by other than lawful means does not hurt or hinder that movement. On the contrary, it strengthens it and drives it underground, and there it festers. There, they perfect their ideas and await their opportunity until the people are sorely pressed by circumstances or some other event makes it feasible for them to show themselves and make their coup.
Let me say this, sir-I see the time is running out-
You are killing it.
Killing time?
Yes.

I hope I am killing the bill also because that is what I am using the time for. Let me put this to my hon. friend: If restrictions of this kind could have prevented communism, what about Russia? Was there ever a country in the world where there were more restrictions, where there were more things that people could not do, where the police force were on the track of almost every man that had an idea? Where did communism come first? Against all the philosophy of Marx, against all the prophecies that he made, communism came in the most backward country and not in the most industrialized country. The reason it came there first was that the policies of the czars drove the communists underground and those communists adopted the very methods the czars adopted to keep them down. When the communists gained power they continued to use the very same method.
That is precisely the reason why we should never touch legislation of this kind in Canada. There is not the slightest doubt in my mind that the best way you could select to put forward and make successful the thing that you are trying to stop would be to pass
Criminal Code
legislation such as this. If you do, you are already spiritual converts to it. To pass this legislation means that you yourself have sanctioned the obscurantism and the suppression which is associated with communism. Having been first spiritually sold to the wrong idea, the other does not matter so much. I say that if people are not allowed to say what they think, to thresh out their ideas in the battle of ideas with other people, and to have it proven to them that their ideas are wrong or right as the case may be, if they are never allowed to air them except amongst their own kind, their ideas do indeed become dangerous.
I repeat that oppressive laws do not stop that which they are designed to stop. As I have said, Russia is an outstanding example of that. I would therefore advise my hon. friends of the Bourbon school to forget some things, if they can, and learn some other things from history. The sponsor will probably argue that we are taking this liberty away because the communists would abuse it. In fact, he said that tonight in his speech. If we allow them liberty, they will abuse liberty. Let them abuse it until they break the law of our country and then we have that law by which we can handle them. You cannot prevent them from abusing liberty without losing liberty yourself, because you are passing a law which will be applicable to anyone in the country who comes under its provisions. Such an argument is as stupid as would be the argument that we should abolish motorcars and highways because bank robbers sometimes use both to get away with their loot.

Before the recess I had asked the minister a question about the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which he said I might ask at this time. I asked him whether there were any plans in his department to extend the operations of that act in order to cover all three of the prairie provinces instead of just the designated area as at the present time. Mr. Chairman, there is no item here for P.F.R.A., which simply means there is no additional amount to be voted. But to answer the question, as I said, there is no intention of bringing in any amendment to the act. Some time ago, during the discussions between the provinces and the dominion, a proposal was made with regard to financing, to the effect that legislation might be set up which would apply the principles of the P.F.R.A. to all of Canada. The present position is that there is no more reason for applying P.F.R.A. to the area outside of what is known as the Palliser triangle in the western provinces than there is for applying it to any other provinces in Canada. I do not think there is any justification for applying it to any area outside of what is known generally as the Palliser triangle. In about June of last year the minister announced that his department, in co-operation with the provinces, was prepared to take on such special projects as may be found desirable outside the boundaries of the desig-

nated areas of P.F.R.A. Is that policy to be followed this year in areas other than those which I have mentioned? The minister knows the case I am leading up to, namely, the projects which have been outlined in the area around Dauphin, where an extensive survey has been made by the P.F.R.A. engineers and plans are being drawn up. Inquiries are being made regularly by the municipalities concerned as to the extent to which the Department of Agriculture here is prepared to act to finance the projects which have been drawn up. Has the minister made any commitments to date to the province of Manitoba, to any municipality or to any person, with regard to the extent to which these projects will be financed, or whether they will be financed at all by the federal Department of Agriculture?

Under "specials" there is a vote of $200,000 in the regular estimates for this coming year, which can be utilized to assist in paying for projects such as, say, the Dauphin project. That would not be carried out as a P.F.R.A. project or even under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, although the engineers who might do the engineering work in connection with the project may be the same engineers as do operate under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
The only way in which the benefits of that vote can be obtained, in say the Dauphin district, would be for the provincial government to assume what is after all their primary responsibility of determining that something ought to be done, and then apply to this government for assistance in the doing of it.
Generally speaking the proposal is that it should be a three-way proposition, the province to pay one-third, the farmers concerned one-third through the municipality or directly, and the government here to assume a similar amount. That is the general plan to be followed, but each project would have to be considered on its merits.

The specific question I asked the minister was whether to date he has made any commitments to Manitoba, to any municipality or to any person in connection with these projects. I am asking that deliberately because I think it is time that it should be cleared up. Rumours are going around. I am not blaming the minister for the rumours, but rumours are going around that commitments have been made, and in order to clear up the thing-

I might say quite definitely that there have been no commitments at all with regard to it. I have stated very definitely to the minister in Manitoba, and have also written him to that effect, and I have

also stated very definitely to the municipalities, that we will undertake absolutely no commitments until we have received some proposal from the province.
Do I take it then that the minister's department has not received a definite proposal from Manitoba? The minister shakes his head.
No, we have not.

I should like to point out to the minister that under the special item to which he referred $200,000 has been allotted for such work as that. That is a small amount in comparison with the amount of work that needs to be done. I am sure that the problem we have in our area is not a singular problem. It exists in other parts of Canada. At this time I would urge the minister when he brings down further supplementary estimates this year to increase the item quite substantially, because if the projects which are now being reviewed in that area are properly undertaken, even if the federal government supplies only one-third of the cost, it will run into a substantial amount of money. May I say at this time it is money that will be well spent, because the amount of damage which has been done through flooding and other causes in that area far exceeds even in one season the whole $200,000 which is in that item.

To shorten the discussion, may I say there is no item here which covers it. There has been an item of $200,000 in the vote for the last two years, and this is the third time it has been put in. We have been saying all the time just exactly what I have said tonight. I have said it here on the floor of the house every session. In other words, there has been $200,000 each year, which makes $400,000 in all which has not been spent at all, although it has been voted each year. Another $200,000 is to be voted this year, and no one has made use of it or even attempted to make use of it in any province in Canada. If no one makes use of it this year, and I have anything to do with it next year, I am going to drop it.

I am glad the minister said that. In the first place, to keep his arithmetic correct, I am not so sure that we have $400,000 because $200,000 was voted two years in a row. If the money is not used it is not there.

It was there and it could have been used. If the proposition had been accepted at the time, and the provincial government had made their representation, in all probability it would have been spent; but I do not think the job is going to cost anything
Supply-Agriculture
like what that amount of money indicates. That amount of money is not all for Manitoba, it is for right across the country, and any figures I can remember would show that the $200,000, which means $600,000 in expenditures, would more than cover the cost of what is proposed.

I do not like to take part in a discussion on the supplementary estimates, but I want to call attention to one point. We are supposed to be a democracy. It seems to me that we are fast becoming an autocracy. We had an exhibition of that this morning in the case of taking in Newfoundland.
Item 573 has to do with the removal of aged apple trees in Nova Scotia and provides the sum of $1 million for that purpose. Item 574 has to do with raspberries in British Columbia and provides the sum of $425,000. The House of Commons is going to get the raspberry back home in the constituencies if we pass items like these in the supplementary estimates. No wonder the toilers and the workers are finding difficulty in buying bread and milk. They are beginning to wonder what the House of Commons is for. We might just as well go home if matters like these are proposed.
At one time Nova Scotia had a market in Britain for about three million barrels of apples, and the government destroyed the whole thing, wiped it right out. Dissolution is coming very shortly. It nearly came the other night, and it might have come. What is the House of Commons for? I do not want to say anything unkind about the minister. He has been very courteous and kind to many of us who have imposed on him by sending so many letters and all that sort of thing. He has been a very hard worker. I do not like this way of doing business. But the House of Commons is giving up responsible government. What I would like to say about this estimate is that I do not think it is necessary to throw preferential trade overboard. That was referred to last night in connection with this business. If we continue to do this, where will we wind up?
I come from a great taxpaying city, one which supplies nearly 31 per cent of the income and sales tax from which this vote comes. Mr. Fielding, who was a good lawyer, said that no sales tax should be over 6 per cent.
What is the House of Commons for? We might as well close up our doors and go home; that is what we might as well do, if we are going to pass items like this. Otherwise we will hear the raspberry song, as we hear it at hockey matches and all that kind of thing. Let me say in conclusion that I have great respect for the Minister

Supply-Agriculture
of Finance, but I do not like to see him doing business this way.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I must ask hon. members to discuss the item before the committee, namely item 573.
I shall take only a few moments. I realize the matter I was discussing only a few moments ago does not come strictly under the procedure of uprooting trees.
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Stick to the item or we will never get through.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to stick to the item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I say a word? I realize that it may be impossible to handle these supplementary estimates tonight. But we do wish to point out to the committee that these are special supplementaries for last year. I appreciate that this is the first occasion upon which the committee has had an opportunity to discuss estimates. But I wonder if it would be possible for members of the committee to restrict their observations this evening to those particular matters which it is not likely may be dealt with in the general estimates.
These are final supplementaries, as I have said, of items which have been passed. All these votes in the main or primary estimates were passed. If we cannot conclude them this evening, we should not try to do so. But I think perhaps with the co-operation of the committee it might be possible to do so if we could restrict our discussions to matters of special importance in connection with these supplementary estimates concerning which there would not be an opportunity for discussion on the main estimates.

Concerning what the minister has said, may I just say this in extenuation of circumstances which have arisen, that while there is a general disposition to have these disposed of at as early a time as possible, I think the situation is attributable to one root cause. I think the reason most hon. members take the opportunity to deal with these matters now is that so many of the estimates are thrown at the committee in the very last days of the session. Many members find it almost impossible, because of the pressure of business, to be able properly to debate them.
I do suggest in all kindness to the minister, and with a constructive desire to have this done properly, that the government should take department after department, and give us a chance during the session, at intervals

here and there, to discuss departmental estimates, instead of having some departments- not just "some"; I should say "many"-facing members for the first time after they have waited about five months to speak on certain items, and finding that they do not have that opportunity before prorogation.
I am not speaking critically at all, but rather from the experience of many years in the house. I think perhaps I have given the root cause of these estimates not going through more quickly tonight.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have only one observation to make, and it is that the estimates were tabled this year, as they were in past years, in good time. However, hon. members are familiar with the rules, and they know that when the government wishes to have a department opened a motion is required to go into supply. Invariably advantage is taken of that to discuss grievances of one kind or another. Opposition members are seldom willing to allow more than one or two departments to be opened on a given date, and the result is that it usually takes two or three weeks to have all the departments opened for discussion. I am not criticizing that practice at all. But I do point out that it is not entirely the fault of the government that an opportunity is not afforded earlier in the session for the discussion of estimates of any department.
Some of them hold them back, and you know that, too.
Order, order.
Sure they do.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Dauphin.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: But I must ask the hon. member not to pursue the subject-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Take it up on the main estimates.

On a point of order, let me point out that I attempted to raise the question when the administration item was before the committee, but the minister advised me to wait until we got to the special item. I have taken his advice on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Perhaps I should not have, but I did. I do not intend to transgress the rules of the house, but I should like to ask
one question if I may.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Go ahead.

And I shall be prepared to drop it then. The minister has indicated

that the same vote will be included under the special item as was included last year and the year before, namely $200,000.
It is in now.

What I want to ask is this: In view of that, and the discussion we have had in connection with this special project in the Dauphin area, will he now say that this government is prepared to finance those projects to the extent of one-third of the cost, whatever it may be?

No, I cannot say that. A submission must be made by the provincial government, and it must be considered first by my department and then presented to council before I can say it will be done. The first step must be taken by the province.

I will stick strictly to the item. Before the dinner recess the minister gave us a very interesting dissertation on the art of moving aged apple trees. He also informed us-and I was glad to find it out- it was a mere coincidence that this million dollars happened to be paid in Nova Scotia at the time a by-election was on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has not been paid yet.

However, I have not had an answer to the first question I asked when the discussion started earlier today, and that is this: Under what authority has this million dollars been paid to these apple-tree owners without the authority of parliament? Without going into all the other details we have heard so far, I think we should have a definite answer to that question. I heard the Minister of Finance say a moment ago that it had not been paid yet; but I understood it had been paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has not been paid; your understanding is incorrect.
I understood the people who owned them had received payment; is that not so?
Except for the part that was not voted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Payment has not been made for anything that has not yet been voted.
He would not understand that.
So far as I can understand, from what the Minister of Agriculture said the other day this million dollars, or a fair part of it, has already been paid out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it has not been paid.

That is the reason I have asked this question. And now, after all this discussion on the matter, which has taken up a great deal of time today, we have the
Supply-Agriculture
Minister of Finance saying that the money has not been paid.
He looked up the book.
If he had said it in the first place-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said it this afternoon.
But, on the basis that it was paid, I was quite unable to understand why it had been done without the authority of parliament for that amount.
Now you understand it.

Because no matter how worthy the purpose may be-and I do not dispute for a moment that the purpose was good-the principle of the government's paying out a large sum of money without having the authority of parliament to do so I think everyone will agree is definitely bad. And as I understood this money was paid, that is what happened in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, it did not.

I do not know just offhand what was in the statement, word for word, that was made in answer to the statement made by the financial critic, the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, when he was speaking earlier in the session, but the intention of the answer was to indicate that we had undertaken to pay the cost of pulling out 240,000 trees. Here I am speaking from memory. There were to be some 60,000 this year and so many next year and so on. The number that was referred to in the agreement that was reached and which was explained to the committee at the time the vote was made this year was 240,000 trees.
We authorized the provincial government to go ahead and pull out those trees, which were covered by the agreement for this year. The provincial government does the job; this government does not do it. They have the trees pulled out and we are presumed to pay the cost. That payment is made to the provincial government. I am not in a position to say whether the provincial government paid the farmers when they made the agreement with them to have the trees pulled out or whether they paid the persons who pulled out the trees. The payments which have been made to the provincial government are quite a different thing. That money will be paid to the provincial government when it is voted here.

We
might just as well have the facts about this. I think the ministers should get together. On February 4 last the minister gave certain information, which is reported on page 261 of Hansard. If I can read English correctly that

Supply-A griculture
information was entirely contrary to what the Minister of Finance is now giving. I then stated that I understood there had been $500,000 in the estimates for last year but that $1,500,000 had been spent. Then the minister interposed a remark and I asked, "Is my arithmetic wrong?" The Minister of Agriculture then replied:
No. The arithmetic is right. But the provision was for the pulling up of 240,000 trees and the pulling was to have taken three years. But it was found that the trees could all be pulled in the one year.
That is absolutely correct.

What I complained about then and what I say now is that we are entitled to have the facts. According to what the Minister of Agriculture said, $500,000 had been voted but $1,500,000 had been spent when there was no authority. That is what he said on February 4. Then on April 1-I do not know whether there is any significance in the date -the Minister of Finance tells us that the money has not been spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let us get this straight. The provincial government was informed that this government would recommend a supplementary estimate to take care of these additional costs. That is what is before the committee now. The money has not been paid because it has not yet been voted. The Minister of Agriculture did not say that it had been paid by the dominion government.
I simply said that the trees had been pulled out.

If the
Minister of Finance will convey that information to the Minister of Agriculture we will be able to get things straightened and get ahead.

There is nothing that needs to be straightened. That statement says that 240,000 trees were to be pulled out and that number has been pulled out. However, there is no suggestion that they have been paid up.
The minister gave that as the reason why the money had been paid.
There was not only the suggestion but the statement on February 4 that they had been paid for. I asked the minister if that was correct and he said it was.
I said that your arithmetic was correct, not that your statement was :orrect.

I just want to restate that my arithmetic was quite simple. I said that $500,000 had been pro-

vided in the estimates but that an additional $1 million had been spent. That was simple enough and the minister said that it was correct. Now we have the Minister of Finance giving an explanation of this, but it comes very late. As I say, it is April 1.

I think we are labouring under a misunderstanding inasmuch as there has been a firm commitment to spend this money which has not been voted. It was made in anticipation that we would vote it. I think that is a sound argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The dominion government
stated to the provincial government that it would recommend a supplementary estimate for an additional $1 million and that is what is being done. Parliament will either vote it or not vote it.

Item agreed to.
574. To provide assistance to the producers of raspberries in British Columbia, under such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council, $425,000.

['The dominion government\nstated to the provincial government that it would recommend a supplementary estimate for an additional $1 million and that is what is being done. Parliament will either vote it or not vote it.']
Will the Minister of Agriculture explain this vote.

I do not think this vote requires any explanation because it has been up at least six times this year. However, I have no objection to making an explanation. A year ago the berry growers of British Columbia found themselves in almost the same position as the apple growers of the Annapolis valley had found themselves in ten years ago. The British had been buying their S02 berries but last year they said that they would not purchase any more. I am perhaps putting it a little too definitely; I should have put it that they suggested that they did not think they would be able to find dollars with which to buy them.
The producers of these berries had considerable acreages last year. Irrespective of what they did about it, it was too late in the season for them to think about doing otherwise. They thought that they probably could find a market for them if we could not prevail upon the British to buy them.
They came to the government and asked us to guarantee their accounts at the bank to an extent which would permit them to get fertilizer, which is the same thing the apple growers were concerned with, then to get baskets or boxes in which the berries are placed when picked, and then to secure barrels in which the berries would be finally placed to be shipped. They said that, unless they could get this advance, under the conditions then existing they would not be in a position to deal with the situation which would develop. So we gave them that guarantee.
That was for the 1948 crop?

We gave them that guarantee in order to assist them to get containers for the 1948 crop and fertilizer as well. The total amount was considerably less than this sum. The berries were picked and they had hopes of being able to sell them. They were put in the barrels but they then found difficulties in marketing the product. They then asked us to deal with the situation on the same basis as we had been dealing with apples and some other products.
As a result there is required this sum of money to pay the guarantee which was consented to by this house last year, and then an added sum in order to pay for the berries themselves. In other words, the government has become responsible for the financing of the berries. I am informed that they have had only $3,000 up to date, but there is $425,000 involved in the cost of putting up the product. We have agreed to pay what was undertaken last year and in addition an amount which will cover the actual cost to the growers so that they can proceed with their operations this year.
We have an undertaking, both from the producers and the provincial government, which has been much concerned with the matter, that acreages will be cut down this year to a point where they will more nearly approach the possible market. I may say that the acreages have been cut down somewhat by the floods and they are undertaking to cut them even more.
Has any help been given in 1949?

This money will go to them immediately and be distributed and in that way some help will be provided. As to what is going to happen in the coming year, they have said, and the provincial government have assured us, that they will not take action this year in the production of SO2 berries which will require assistance.
What portion of last year's crop has been sold?

I cannot say that offhand. There are some berries now stored in the United States for which they say they will have a market. My understanding is that, so far as the producers of these berries are concerned, they only had $3,000 out of a total cost of $425,000.
I am not criticizing the vote.

I am very glad to know that Vancouver South is at last producing a few berries. The berries that are being sold are what are known as S02 berries. They are in solution. The berries that are in storage in
Supply-Agriculture
the United States are frozen berries. I appreciate very much the assistance of the hon. member for Vancouver South. I think the minister should go further and point out that we are now being paid 12 cents a pound under the latest order. It is a very small proportion of our crop. During the war we were encouraged by the government to increase our production of berries in the province of British Columbia, and we did so. Eighty-five per cent of the berries are grown in my riding. When the foreign exchange regulations came into effect, we had no market for our surplus. We put our surplus berries into what we call S02. It is a solution that preserves them for future canning purposes. The rest of our berries were sold or stored in cold storage in the United States. We have sold some berries over there, and some are not sold. I want to say on behalf of the people of my riding, where 85 per cent of the berries are grown, that we think we have received a very fair deal from the government because they have taken over a surplus, as well as giving us fertilizer. They took over the surplus at a price less than we were accustomed to receiving in wartime. Speaking from memory I believe the price is 12 cents a pound.
One thing that we do object to is the delay. Prior to the war we were getting 4$ to 5 cents of the total cost for berries. During the war we paid 4J to 5J cents a pound for picking berries. As the minister stated, a large percentage of the producers of berries in the Fraser valley have not to date received the cost of picking, let alone a profit or return to themselves that they might use for taxes, living purposes, or anything else. I think that the minister has been very fair. I do not suggest that there is any fault on the part of his department, but there is definitely fault on the part of the treasury board and the Department of Finance because they should expedite payment of this money so that the farmers of the Fraser valley can at least get the cost of their production returned.
Why was this matter not dealt with under the Agricultural Prices Support Act? Could the payments not have been made under that act instead of by a special vote such as this?

It is not a floor price that is being put under berries. As a matter of fact, the greater part of it is to pay for the containers the cost of which we guarantee. It is not putting a price under berries in that sense at all. As has been suggested by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, we pay 12 cents for the actual berries that are in the containers, but the part of the payment which forms the basis of the vote does not have to do with price. It has to do with the guaran-

Supply-External Affairs tee we gave so that they could go to the bank last year and finance the containers and fertilizers.
Would the minister explain to the committee the subsidy on fertilizer to these British Columbia berry growers? What is the policy of the government in that regard?
It is exactly the same as it was with regard to the containers. We guarantee their accounts at the bank, and they purchase fertilizer and use it.

The full
amount?
Yes.
No.
Well, I do not know that it is quite the full amount.
Item agreed to.
577.	International civil aviation organization, $196,200.

There are two votes for the international civil aviation organization, No. 577 in the amount of $196,200, and No. 656 on page 11, in the amount of $122,000. Will whoever is acting for the Secretary of State for External Affairs explain what those two votes are, and why there are two votes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By decision of the second assembly of the international civil aviation organization, the Canadian government was assigned fifteen units on a scaled contribution, out of a total of 304J units for the period July 1, 1948, to December 31, 1948, and 15 units out of 305J for the calendar year 1949. By decision of the assembly the fiscal year of the organization has been changed to conform with the calendar year. The fiscal year previously was from July 1 to June 30. Accordingly the last fiscal period would be the six months from July 1 to December 31, 1.948, and thereafter the calendar year, 1949. The payment due by Canada, based on the total budget, for the six months is $66,004, and for the calendar year from January 1, 1949, to December 31, 1949, is $130,099, making a total of $196,103. It is desired that the amount of $196,200, covered by the contribution for the remaining six months of 1948, and the contribution for the calendar year 1949, be provided in these further supplementary estimates.
In advance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite correct; it is really payment in advance.

What about the second item?
[Mr Gardiner ]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I might take that up later.
May I ask what the total funds of the organization amount to, and how many countries contribute to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I have not that information here, but when we reach the main estimates of the Department of External Affairs I will make sure that information is available.
Do you know the officers of the organization?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not got them here.

There are forty-five nations in the organization. They are all assessed on the basis of the number of aeroplanes they fly and the number of route miles flown. The organization is international. The president is an American, and I think some eleven nations are represented on the board of the organization.
Do they issue a report?
No.
Is this the item under which we should discuss civil aviation within Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. This is the international civil aviation organization which controls routes and makes the rules for international flying. I am afraid I am not too competent to answer the question, but the Secretary of State for External Affairs unfortunately cannot be here this evening. He had to leave for Washington this afternoon.

I had no idea this was coming up tonight, and if it covers Canadian civil aviation I have something to say on the matter, because now you have to be a Rhodes scholar to run your own private plane. I think the hon. member for Vancouver South knows something about what I am referring to. Is this the item under which we should discuss that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so. I would hope my hon. friend would not feel he had to discuss it on these supplementary estimates. I will bring his remarks to the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and when we reach a similar item on the main estimates that will be a good time to bring it up.
As I understand it the international civil aviation organization is one of the organizations set up under the United Nations, with headquarters in Montreal?
That is correct.
Apparently the cost to Canada each year is over $100,000?
Yes.

We have not had a statement
for some time with respect to Canadian government policy on international aviation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will remember, I think, that the first statement on this subject was made by the former Prime Minister on April 2, 1943. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce made a lengthy statement of policy on March 17, 1944, in which he set out Canada's plan for an international air transport convention, which was subsequently considered by the various nations meeting together, and some of the suggestions made by Canada were not adopted. I do not believe there has been a statement of government policy since 1944. There must have been many changes in the meantime, and I would ask the minister whether it would be possible for the house to be given at an early date a statement of the government's view at the present time in regard to international aviation.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has nothing to do with that matter now, as my hon. friend knows, but I shall be glad to call it to the attention of the Minister of Transport.
I think it very important that we should know exactly what Canada now stands for in the field of international aviation.

Now that we are on external affairs- I do not know whether this is quite relevant to the item- I was wondering whether there were any aeroplanes thrown in or left in the basement of the $85,000 house we bought in Cuba the other day, where we need an ambassador about as much as we need a third leg.
I understood the minister to say there were 305 units?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are 305J.
That means $8,800 per unit, or over $2,500,000, to run this organization for one year. What does it do to spend that amount of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am not in a position to give very much information; it is not my department. As the committee knows, on these final supplementary estimates it is not always possible for all the ministers to be here. When the main estimates are under consideration I am sure either the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Minister of Transport will be prepared to go into the matter as fully as possible, but I am afraid I am not in a position to give the information for which my hon. friend asks.

The cost of this organization seems to be mounting very quickly. In 1947-48 the appropriation was $25,001, and
Supply-External Affairs the expenditures were even less. The point I have in mind was just made by the hon. member for Calgary West. The traveling expenses and other expenditures in connection with our representation at some of these conferences is becoming quite an item. In 1947-48 the traveling expenses of Canadians attending international conferences amounted to $246,000 and other expenditures to almost $122,000, or a total of about $367,000. These are not expenditures incidental to membership in these organizations; they represent traveling expenses and other expenditures while at these conferences. This is another item showing that expenditures in connection with these matters are mounting at an unusually rapid rate.

We are asked to vote $196,000 for this organization for a period of eighteen months, after which I presume there will be a vote from year to year. These are large amounts, and it seems to me this House of Commons should have a report showing how the money is spent. We are asked to vote money but we do not know how it is spent, we do not know what officers they have, we do not know what duties they perform or anything else, and I believe we should be furnished with that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that quite a full report was given to the external affairs committee of this house last session, and I would hope that a similar report might be given this year. In the main estimates last year there was an item for Canada's membership in this organization, which, as an hon. gentleman opposite has pointed out, is one of the organizations set up under the United Nations. This is part of our club dues, so to speak, to belong to the organization. Opinions may differ; perhaps we should get out of some of these things, but for the moment we are in them. My hon. friend is quite right; parliament should have information as to how the moneys are spent, but I am sure he will understand when I say that I do not think the final supplementaries for the year are the best occasion to go into that question. I am handicapped by the fact that, through no fault of his own, the Secretary of State for External Affairs cannot be here this evening. I have given the basis on which this vote is made up; it is 15/305.5 of the total expenses for six months of the past year and to bring it on a current basis.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I wish to express my support of this item we are now considering, and I am happy to do so. I rise to say this word in order to call attention to the item, in view of the remarks I shall have to make on the next item.

I want to draw the attention of the committee to this item. Like the last speaker, I have no fault to find with it, and I am sure that if the lady mentioned here has no other source of revenue, it is little enough. I am sure also that no means test will be involved. But at this stage I should like to point out that there are a great many civil servants who do not quite fall into the glittering category which included the late gentleman in question, and who are at present receiving as little as $40 per month by way of superannuation. It might be well to draw attention to the terrific contrast provided by this item.
