Superannuation and retirement benefits-
579.	Government's contribution to the superannuation fund-further amount required, $320,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This item calls for a further contribution from the government to the superannuation fund. I could hope that this would be for the purpose of granting a cost of living bonus or other supplement to superannuated civil servants, but the Minister of Finance has given a negative reply to my appeal and that of others so often that I imagine such is not the case. The minister writes letters, not only to people down in Digby-Annapolis-Kings but also to associations of superannuated civil servants across the country, who make their appeals to him. As the minister can quite well imagine, these people have copies of his letters made and placed in the hands of those of us who are interested in their case. There is nothing humorous in these letters I refer to; rather they state the minister's reasons for not acceding to the request. In the main the minister usually compares the superannuation act of this country with the superannuation acts of various other countries, and is able to point out that in many if not all respects the act here is as good as or better than the others.
Well, is it not?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It is-now. I want to support what the minister says in that connection, but it does seem to me that in the answers the minister has made to these retired civil servants he has failed to cover the point about which we are making repre-
[Mr. Abbott.J
sentations. We are concerned about the people who worked at a time when the superannuation act was not as good as it now is. They are the people who worked at a time when the wages or salaries they received-and the pension is based on their wages or salary-were hopelessly inadequate.
As I say, the minister compared our superannuation act with the basic superannuation acts of other countries. I should like him to give consideration to the fact that in the United Kingdom, in addition to the superannuation act, there is what is known as the Pensions Increase Act. That act was first passed in 1944 and it was amended in 1947. The sole purpose of the Pensions Increase Act of the United Kingdom was to provide supplementary payments to retired civil servants-note that, persons already retired- whose pensions are in the lower brackets. These people make that request of the government, and it is a request that has been made on the floor of the house from time to time. Despite the repeated negative replies, I hope the minister will even yet give consideration to the matter.
If I may shorten the discussion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to send across to the minister copies of the Pensions Increase Act, 1944, of the United Kingdom, together with the amending bill of 1947 and certain other official information. I am going to ask him to study it himself or have his departmental officials study it or refer it to the advisory committee on matters relating to the superannuation act. I hope before this session goes much further these people-not necessarily the whole gamut of retired civil servants, but certainly those in the lower brackets-might get something of what they deserve.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thank you; I shall be glad to look at it.

I do hope, Mr. Chairman, that the minister will give further consideration to this question. Several times in the past he has turned down the request of the superannuated civil servants, and I have thought he did so in a very short way. In my opinion their suggestions merit the most careful consideration, for these reasons: During the years on which the superannuation is based for many of those retired civil servants, they did not receive their statutory increases. Further than that, their salaries were cut. Of course, the superannuation is now paid- I am not talking to the Minister of Labour.
I was just asking who cut the salaries of the civil servants.

The superannuation is based on the salary received over a period of years.

These people are now met with a greatly increased cost of living. There is no doubt whatever that many of them, certainly those receiving small amounts, are having a very difficult time.
Another reason why Canada should do something for these people is that, apparently, the United States provided for an increase a year or two ago. As the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has pointed out, something along the same line has been done in the United Kingdom.
And in Saskatchewan as well.

I think the request is very well set out in a letter written by the superannuated federal civil servants of Canada, Vancouver branch. I propose to quote two or three paragraphs from that letter. It reads as follows:
Prior to 1924 the parliament of that day found it necessary to provide assistance to those of its employees who, owing to age or infirmity, were no longer able to perform their duties. The Calder Act was passed for this purpose, under which those retired were given back all their accumulated contributions under the old retirement act, and, in addition, were paid a fairly generous pension.
Another paragraph of that letter reads as follows:
There was no general upward revision of salaries from 1924 until recent years: therefore, it is quite evident that the superannuation received by those who retired during that period are based on conditions prevailing some twenty-five years ago. This fact, we claim, nullifies to a great extent the object of superannuation, which is to provide those retired with life's simple necessities during their declining years. Instead our superannuation has been reduced by over fifty per cent.
Of course, by that statement they mean the cost of living has risen to such a height that their superannuation only purchases half the amount it could formerly.
The letter continues as follows:
We further assert that it is not logical to compare our superannuation contributions with other forms of industrial investments. Those who purchase annuities, stocks, bonds, etc., do so voluntarily, while we were compelled to subscribe to the fund as a condition of employment-
I submit that is a very important point. This is important, too:
-with the assurance that it met our financial security on retirement.
In other words, that they would receive this superannuation and that the amount of it would be sufficient to enable them to live.
The letter goes on to state:
However, the drastic increase in living costs today, through no fault of ours, very greatly reduces the benefits we would have received had conditions remained normal.
Consideration has been given to the increased cost of living for others and many people have received increased salaries. We
Supply-Finance
have done that for ourselves in this House of Commons. I cannot understand why the minister should just brush these requests aside and refuse to have an investigation made of the plight of the superannuated federal civil servants.

Before coming to Ottawa to attend this session, along with other members of parliament from Vancouver, I was asked to attend a meeting called by superannuated civil servants. We listened to the difficulties they are experiencing because of rising living costs. It seems to me that we should at least look at this matter in a realistic and humanitarian way. The mere fact that these people are superannuated does not mean that the cost of living does not go up for them in the same way as it would if they were working.
I submit all our superannuation and other retirement allowances should be based and, indeed, must be based on some real standard of living at the time when the rates were set. If they are not so based, they do not mean anything. It is assumed that a person on superannuation, whether that superannuation is large or small, will be sufficient to provide a living, if not on the same standard as when working, at least on a standard approaching that condition. When conditions arise over which these people have no control, conditions which wipe out half of their superannuation, surely we should not insist that they have no claim for redress.
Earlier in the evening we were discussing a question that related to the growth of communism and what to do about it. I do not know of any better way to create discontent. When discontent is once created you do not know where it will lead. I do not know of any better way to create discontent than to compel people to live on an income that does not give them anything like the standard of living they once had, and that they would have now if they were employed, and that their neighbours enjoy. Indeed, there should be an investigation into all low income cases to find out what their income really is now in terms of 1945 or 1941 dollars. I would suggest to the minister that, particularly at this time when we are so much disturbed about where to dispose of our surplus food products, we should see to it that our own people here in Canada are not suffering for want of the food that we do not know what to do with. To allow the thing to continue does not make sense; indeed, it makes nonsense.

I should like to say a word on this item and to support what has been said by the previous speakers. Since I first received letters from superannuated civil servants I have been deeply concerned about

Supply-Finance
their situation. I have before me the minister's answer in a sessional paper of January 26, 1948, when he based his refusal to grant any increase to superannuated civil servants upon the ground that the government does not consider that it would be fair or proper to single out its former employees for special assistance. Before that he had made reference to those who had fixed incomes arising out of investments and other savings.
That argument seemed to have some principle in it, and yet I could not feel that the decision of the minister was right. There are a large number of superannuated civil servants who get a very small pension. The reason may be-it certainly is-that, under the act, by their length of service or their rate of pay before the war, they did not qualify for any more. But according to the answer to a question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which is to be found on page 584 of Hansard, the actual fact is that approximately 1,400 pensioned civil servants get less than $40 a month, and approximately 2,200 widows of former civil servants get less than $40 a month.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The number is 2,319.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says that the number is 2,319. Of course there are many more who get amounts ranging up to $100 a month or over. I could list all the figures, but I am particularly concerned with those in that very low income group. I sought for the answer to the minister's argument in that paper of January 26. It is quite obvious that the minister will not want to set a wrong precedent in this connection, and I think that is his real fear.
I looked up the debates on the pension increase given in Great Britain in 1944, and I found there very clearly the principle that they went on in increasing the pensions for their former civil servants, on account of the increased cost of living. I want to quote to the minister what Sir John Anderson, who was then the chancellor of the exchequer, said in this connection, because it will give him a principle upon which he can find his way around the argument that he advanced a year ago in refusing the application of the superannuated civil servant.
It is quite obvious that we have financed the war to a certain extent by inflating the currency, a certain amount by borrowing and a certain amount by taxation. We all share that inflation together; but it hits very hard particularly those in the groups to which I have made reference tonight, namely, those who are getting less than $40 a month. I do not think it is at all unfair that they should be relieved of the joint burden that we all

carry in respect of inflation of the currency. I believe that is the view that was taken in Great Britain when this matter was up because Sir John Anderson said, as reported on page 1761 of volume 367 of the United Kingdom debates:
That will be essentially the approach which the government propose to make, that is, to take account, as in the legislation following the last war, of the position of the pensioner and to provide increases for the lower ranges of pensions, in order, so far as may be practicable, to mitigate really severe hardship.
That was the principle behind their increase and it is one I suggest the minister could follow without in any way setting a bad precedent or making a bad comparison with others who may also have been hit by the same problem.
I want to call to the attention of the Minister of Finance two other things that Sir John Anderson said. He said:
In the view of the government, the arguments for and against doing something were still fairly evenly and nicely balanced, but, on the whole, the government considered that there was a case for some action.
I think that is exactly the position that we are in in this House of Commons. Where the arguments are nicely and evenly balanced there might well be some action. The last thing I want to call to the minister's attention, again quoting from Sir John Anderson, is his answer to the minister's own argument in refusing the increase:
For example, the recipient of interest on government stock cannot claim an increase on similar grounds, although there may be hardship in both cases. But the government rightly take a sympathetic view of the difficulties of their own pensioned servants.
With respect to these in the very low categories of pension this government could very easily take a sympathetic view of their own pensioners without in any way disturbing the relationship of other groups in the country.

Owing to the very large number of retired superannuated civil servants who live on Vancouver island, I should like to express my sincere hope that the government will be able to consider some recommendations which have been made by the previous speakers, and will try to take some action in order to relieve the difficult conditions under which I know personally many of these superannuated civil servants are now trying to exist.

Private industry in this country is arranging for life insurance and old age pensions, and is setting an example to the government. Men and women who some years ago chose the civil service as their vocation certainly could not contemplate the cost of living of today. I do not suppose it would

cost the taxpayers of Canada a great deal to give common-sense consideration to this matter, comparing pensions with the present-day cost of living; and without any more ado about it and waste of the taxpayers' money in long arguments this government, in a pure, cold and businesslike manner, could grant these people the necessary increase which would provide them with a livelihood in keeping with present-day conditions. It could cut down on some other nonsensical expenditures, such as publishing a thousand volumes in French and English of a military dictionary at a cost of $25,000, and turning out at a cost of $30,000 circulars to industry advising them how to start suggestion boxes in their factories. If they will just provide the money where it is necessary no taxpayer will growl about it. They should at least be willing to keep pace with the example set by private industry.

As might be expected in a city the size of Toronto-and the same would apply to Montreal-there are many retired and pensioned civil servants. Before coming to Ottawa for this session I was approached, as were the hon. members for Vancouver South, Winnipeg North Centre, Nanaimo and Vancouver-Burrard, all of which ridings are populous. Those who approached me were retired federal civil servants. I need refer to only two or three classes, and only briefly to them, because the matter has been well covered by those who have preceded me. One of these classes is that of postal station employees and the letter carriers and a number of wives of deceased postal employees whose husbands in their lifetime paid into a pension fund and who are now receiving pensions. Some of those men were customs officials, while others were employees of the Department of Public Works.
There are large numbers of these in a city the size of Toronto. Those who paid into a superannuation fund had moneys deducted from their salaries at the values of that time. However a pension founded on the moneys received by such civil servants in their working days today does not go nearly as far as money would go at the time the deductions were made.
I am not thoroughly familiar with the pension set-up, but I have been wondering if the pensions of civil servants of former years had been increased by a cost of living bonus, as applies to civil servants who are in employment today. If that is not done I should think that the pensions received by civil servants or the widows of former civil servants should be supplemented by a cost of living bonus to bring up the value of their
Supply-Finance
pensions to what it should be, in view of the high cost of living today.
I know the minister has a problem on his hands. But the matter has been so well presented by the hon. members I mentioned a moment ago, and as it had been pointed out to myself, I felt bound to support what had been said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no doubt we will be discussing this very important question on other occasions at this session. I have only this to say. As in the constituencies of other hon. members who have spoken, there are a great many superannuated civil servants in my own riding. But there are also a great many other retired persons who are not superannuated civil servants, who have sought to provide their own superannuation, or who may be getting pensions, small or otherwise, from pension funds. I have not been able to see on what basis the government could improve the pension position of its own employees-and, mind you, a pension is a contractual obligation-and not give comparable treatment to other taxpayers; because it is the taxpayers of Canada who contribute to these superannuation payments.
That is the difficulty the government faces; that is the difficulty the Minister of Finance faces. He must, if he can, be fair to everyone in the community. I have not yet been able to see-taking my own constituency as an example-how I can improve the pension position of those who happen to be retired civil servants and, out of the public funds, not make a comparable improvement in the position of other retired persons who are not the recipients of superannuation payments but who are suffering from exactly the same hardship as a result of increased living costs. That is the problem with which we are faced.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think there are one or two matters which should be straightened out here. Perhaps it has been my fortune to deal with as many of these cases as any member in the committee. It is a difficult problem, and there can be no doubt that	hardship-real hardship-is
being suffered by some of these superannuated civil servants.
But I could not sit here tonight and listen to the opposition without recalling a time when I sat in another part of this chamber- a little higher up-and watched this condition being caused. If anyone here cares to analyse carefully cases where hardship is being suffered he will find that, almost without exception, it is due to the policy carried out in this country between the years 1930 and 1935.

Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would develop that a little further.
Call for Mr. Pickering.

About time there was a
change in Ottawa West.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Salaries were cut 10 per
cent; all promotions were stopped; all reclassifications were stopped. The cumulative effect of that over a period of five years is quite an item, when one is considering superannuation; because superannuation, depending upon the grouping, is based upon either the last five years of salary or the last ten years. To the ones superannuated in the thirties, it worked out that most of them came under the last five years of salary. That, plus the time factor, was the item taken into account in fixing the superannuation.
Hon. members will find, if they care to study this matter-however unpleasant it may be to them now to recognize it-that that is the cause of this condition. The condition is there. The hardship is being suffered mostly by civil servants who were superannuated before that condition was corrected, before increases in pay were given back.
Whatever the cause, I am interested to note the change in hon. members opposite, I hope that it is in fact a real change in their point of view. One cannot have witnessed it at close hand without feeling a little sensitive and somewhat strongly on the point.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: By all means.
The hon. member has referred to a cause; what remedy would he pres-scribe?|

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I shall come to that.
It was prescribed in 1935.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I shall come to that. As the hon. member for New Westminster points out, it is very necessary to keep the Liberal party in power, if civil servants are to get anything like a fair deal.

We are trying to help you
out.
You certainly are.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I appreciate that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
You are blaming the dead
hand of the past.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have not come to my point yet.
You are taking a long time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Well, I am taking sufficient time to put it clearly before the committee,

because it warrants that degree of attention and care.
I have referred to the conditions that caused this situation. I have said that hardship is being suffered. There is no doubt of that. I recognize the difficulties and no useful purpose can be served by brushing them aside. My suggestion is that we bear in mind that roughly speaking the superannuation fund is made up one-half by contributions by the employees and one-half by contributions by the dominion government. I am aware that arguments can be raised about those figures, but that seems to be the fairest figure that can be arrived at.
My suggestion is that the dominion government is perfectly justified in adding to the half that it is paying on the basis that that would be a contribution for the ex-employee. The government has taken into account the increases in the cost of living of its employees so why should it not consider the ex-employees in so far as that part of the fund which it contributes is concerned.
That is the only workable solution I have been able to develop. I think it has the virtue of meeting the difficulty that undoubtedly does exist with respect to all those others in receipt of fixed incomes. I urge that that solution be carefully examined and action taken.

I do not want to get into an argument as to whether the Conservative government in the days of R. B. Bennett or the present Liberal administration is more to blame for the present plight of superannuated civil servants. Undoubtedly the cutting of salaries had something to do with the basis on which superannuation is calculated, but on the other hand the present administration must take the responsibility for the increase in the cost of living.
In my own province and in my own riding we have a rather glaring example of what exists. On the one hand, there are superannuated civil servants of the province of Saskatchewan who are in receipt of a cost of living bonus from the provincial government which ignores the argument of the Minister of Finance that this is a contractual obligation, and on the other hand there are superannuated civil servants of the dominion government who have not received any additional bonus or allowance to help them over this particularly expensive period in their lives.
I do not want to go over the arguments that have been advanced. I simply want to join those members of my own party and of the Progressive Conservative party who have pleaded tonight with the Minister of Finance to find seme way out of this impasse to help
the 2,000-odd superannuated civil servants who are in the lower pension brackets.

I was interested in the explanation given to the committee by the Minister of Finance. I am prepared to be corrected if my analysis of what he said is wrong, but I take it that according to the Minister of Finance the government is under the obligation of aiding and assisting all citizens of this country who are in the position of being retired.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have an old age pension law.

We have an old age pension law, but I think the minister is placing that in a higher category than it deserves. I would hardly consider the pensions paid as being classified as retirement allowances. No one could retire on $30 or $40 per month these days.	.
In his explanation of his position and his difficulties the minister said that it would oe unfair to look after the former employees of the government and not at the same time look after all former employees of all private enterprises in the country. It seems to me that to carry the argument to that point is illogical and ridiculous, without using the word "ridiculous" in anything but a deferential sense toward the minister. It is his arguments that are ridiculous; he has not yet become so. I have never heard a poorer case made for a government that is dodging its responsibility.
The position is that the superannuated civil servants were not the employees of any private corporation in the country, they were our employees. Our government, our people employed them to carry out our work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why should they be in a privileged position?

They are in the position that every employee of any company would be in with regard to the company that had formerly employed him. If these people had been employed by a private corporation they would be justified in going to that corporation and asking for assistance. But these people were not employed by a private corporation, they were employed by the federal government. They are asking the federal government, and I think they are justified, to take their case into consideration.
If any company having a superannuation plan were approached by its former employees with the plea that the superannuation they were receiving was not sufficient to meet the high cost of living and that therefore further assistance should be given, that company might turn around and say, "Why should we do this for you when the government does
Supply-Finance
not do anything for its superannuated civil servants?" They would have an equally just case. With that kind of argument nobody ever gets anywhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about the fellow who worked for himself and not for a corporation?

Under the existing system the fellow who worked for himself would have nowhere to go if he had not enough to live on and were no longer able to work. But under the system that my party envisages he would. However, we are not dealing with that at the moment, we are dealing with the situation in which the Minister of Finance finds himself. No amount of wriggling or trying to place this matter in some other category is going to deviate this committee from presenting the case of the superannuated civil servant. The Minister of Finance will have to put up a more logical argument before we will be satisfied with the justice of his position.

I want to say only a sentence or two and what I want to say to the minister will be in the form of a pleasant warning. I gather that the people for whom I spoke in the short speech I made in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne are covered. I refer to such persons as the mounted police.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe they have a separate pension plan.

Then I will say
nothing else.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is closely analogous to the military pension plan.

The governments have always said that they were simply civil servants. The Bennett government, of whom the hon. member for Ottawa West is so fond, and this government have always given the same answer. So I shall leave it for the moment and try to be here at the proper time. May I close by saying that I do not think that these retired civil servants, particularly those in the lower brackets, can be decently dealt with by just using a rule of thumb. We cannot just bracket them with all other persons who have put their savings in corporation pension schemes, saving plans and so on. I think there is a distinction between governmental employees and others. Of course, I assume it is a contractual relationship. When all these people went to work for the government they no doubt joined the scheme, and made their contributions. I have no doubt that it was not at all secret; it was a public matter and was conducted on the highest plane. It seems to me that the basis of the appeal is one of need, not of contract.

Supply-Finance
I think the government should endeavour to look at it from that point of view. It is a borderline matter, and we should adopt the same rule that is adopted in all provinces with respect to workmen's compensation, that the benefit of the doubt goes to the workman. The same rule should be applied in our thinking with respect to many of these now fairly elderly people who have been trying to get along, and particularly those who are unable to do any other work. If you could look after them it would be of some help. It should be done on the basis of their great need without too much regard to the dotting of the i's and the crossing of the t's, and the exact letter of the contract.

For a great many years now it has been the custom of the government to reward those who have grown old in the public service, and who have come to the days when their strength is not so great. There must have been a reason why the government did that. The reason must have been that the government felt that people who had served their time in the employ of the government were entitled to consideration in their declining years.
I see no reason why, in times of high prices like these, people of that sort should be called upon to sacrifice a certain amount of the security which had been guaranteed to them through the years. I think that constitutes the main reason for going out of our way far enough by a bonus or some other means, to see that such people do not have to suffer a part of the consequences of rising prices for which they had no responsibility whatsoever.
Members of the opposition have expressed themselves in favour of an additional reward for the superannuated civil servants. I think they have pretty well said all that there is to be said. I desire to associate myself with them in the remarks which they have made, the arguments which they have advanced, and the suggestions they have offered to the minister that something should be done for the superannuated civil servants.
A moment ago one of the members of the C.C.F. party said that in the plan of life which they visualize provision would be made for all such people, whether or not they had been employed by the government. May I say to the minister that in the plan which Social Crediters envisage ample provision will be made for the people who have spent their lives in making the country what it is. It is not appropriate that I should say at the present time just what those provisions will be, but I will say that the question we should keep our eyes upon in dealing with all such questions as this one of adequate

remuneration for superannuated civil servants-the important question-is how much goods can this country produce? Is Canada able to produce enough food, clothing, and shelter to supply these people with the needs of life? If so, then let us devise the financial means whereby that food, clothing, shelter, with other necessities, can be made available to these people in an amount sufficient to provide for them comfortably in their later years.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to say a further word to impress upon the minister why it is that we are having quite so much to say about this matter tonight. I think he will agree with me that more members of the house have taken part in the discussion than has ever been the case when this item has been before the house-at least in the years that I have been here. The reason that we are pressing him so hard is that not since January, 1948, has any question on the floor of the house, or any appeal from these organizations, met with the assurance that the matter would be reconsidered.
May I remind the Minister of Finance, and the other ministers who are here tonight- and I am sure we are all glad that so many members of the cabinet, including the Prime Minister, have been listening to this important discussion-that the agitation to do something for these people began late in 1945 or early in 1946, when the cost of living first started to mount, and was carried on pretty strenuously and continuously through 1946 and 1947. During those years our plea to the former Minister of Finance, to the present Minister of Finance, and to the government as a whole, was to give consideration to this matter. It took a long time to get the government to agree to consider it. Broadcast from St. John's, Newfoundland:
Commentator: I am speaking to you now from Government House, in St. John's, the official residence of all governors of Newfoundland since about 1832, when responsible government was first introduced into the island. In this building all our governors and administrators of government since that time have taken their oaths of allegiance and office, and it is eminently fitting that here should be sworn in also the first Lieutenant Governor of this new province of Canada.
Present in these rooms are His Honour the Lieutenant Governor Designate, the Honourable Albert Walsh, K.C., and His Lordship the Chief Justice, the Honourable Sir Edward Emerson, who will administer the oaths. Also present are the judges of the Supreme Court; the heads of the various churches; representatives of Canada, the United States, France, Portugal; the mayor of St. John's, permanent heads of the local government; the Prime Minister Designate and his colleagues; representative citizens and their wives, and members of the local and foreign press, numbering in all about one hundred.
The ceremony today will be a brief but none the less impressive one. It will open with the singing of the Ode to Newfoundland by a choir under the direction of Mr. Robert McLeod. Following this you will hear the reading of the commission of the Lieutenant Governor. Then follows the highlight of this afternoon's ceremony, when the Chief Justice, Sir Edward Emerson, will administer the oaths of allegiance and office to the first Lieutenant Governor, the Honourable Sir Albert Walsh, ICC. Following this, the Honourable Colin Gibson, a member of the Canadian government, will present to His Honour
token Canadian citizenship papers, and, in accepting on behalf of the people of Newfoundland, Sir Albert will reply. This will conclude the ceremony at St. John's. The proceedings at Ottawa will follow immediately.
Now, all is in readiness for the ceremony here at Government House.
Ladies and gentlemen, the Ode to Newfoundland.

On presentation of token certificate of citizenship to Sir Albert Walsh, Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland:

speakeroldname: Hon. Colin Gibson (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
Your Honour, it is a great privilege for me, as a representative of the Prime Minister and the people of Canada, to be here today in St. John's to take part in this confederation ceremony.
We welcome the people of Newfoundland who today become equal partners with us in the development of the northern part of the American continent.
In recognition of your entry into our confederation I have much pleasure in presenting to you, sir, this certificate of Canadian citizenship, which has been specially prepared to mark this occasion. As you will see, it certifies that every Newfoundland British subject coming within the relevant provisions of the Canadian Citizenship Act adds to his status as a British subject that of being a Canadian citizen, and that he or she is entitled to all rights, powers and privileges, and subject to all obligations, duties and liabilities, to which a natural-born Canadian citizen is entitled or subject.
I can assure you, sir, that all the people of Canada join with me in extending to the people of Newfoundland a welcome into our Canadian family.

Hon. Mr. Gibson, on behalf of the people of Newfoundland I am happy to welcome you on the occasion of your visit to Newfoundland to take part in this ceremony as the representative of the Prime Minister and the people of Canada.
The certificate of citizenship which you have presented to the people of Newfoundland, through me, shows that all of us now have a new status, that of Canadian citizens, which entitles us to rank equally with all other Canadian citizens throughout all Canada. This new citizenship is in addition to the status which we have enjoyed in common, the status of British subjects. I am glad to accept this certificate, and can assure you that the people of Newfoundland who

will enjoy the privileges of this new citizenship will faithfully discharge their duties as citizens.
I am sure that all the people of Newfoundland wish me to express through you to the people of Canada our appreciation of the welcome which you have extended on their behalf on this historic occasion, and to extend best wishes to a people with whom we have for many years been so closely associated.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should like to direct my first words today to the people of the new Canadian province of Newfoundland. I know I am speaking for the people of the other nine provinces when I say that we welcome you warmly as fellow Canadians.
In greeting you as fellow citizens we do not feel that you in Newfoundland have ever been strangers. In peace we have been happy to live and work beside you. In two wars we have been glad you were in our company and we in yours. We have the same traditions and the same way of life. We are both proud of our association in the British commonwealth of nations. We have shared, and continue to share, a common loyalty to His Majesty the King.
At this time, when we are taking a major step in the life of Newfoundland and of all Canada, the people of the nine older provinces and those of Newfoundland are equally aware that one circumstance that has contributed to union is our common loyalty to His Majesty the King. That common loyalty will continue to be one of the most important forces in the life of our united nation. With those thoughts in mind, I asked His Excellency the Governor General to convey a message this morning-the first full day of the new union- to His Majesty King George VI. The message reads as follows:
On the occasion of the entry of Newfoundland into confederation as a province of Canada I send to Your Majesty, on behalf of the government and people of Canada, the expression of our devoted loyaltv. together with our sincere good wishes to you and to Her Majesty the Queen. The people of Canada, those of Newfoundland and those of the other provinces of Canada, now one nation under the crown, are happy to learn of Your Majesty's improvement in health, and join in wishing you a speedy recovery.
The union we celebrate today was not concluded without the most careful consideration by representatives of both Canada and Newfoundland.

In 1947, when the delegation from your national convention came to Ottawa to see if a satisfactory basis could be found for the political union, we were pleased. We had no hesitation in making it clear that we would welcome union. But we recognized that the decision was one for you to make yourselves. We were happy when you, the people of Newfoundland, decided by a free vote that you favoured union. And we are happy today to have the union completed.
In welcoming you as partners in the Canadian nation, we of the rest of Canada feel that you are joining a good country, a country of which you will come to be as proud as we are. Canada is a country with a distinctive character and distinctive qualities. Our nation in its origin was a union of two great races that have joined their talents without merging their identities. The union includes peoples of many other national origins. Our country covers a vast area between two oceans, with great differences of soil and climate and industry. But from end to end of Canada there is an ever-deepening sense of community of interest and of purpose. We have a common pride in being Canadians. We are proud of Canada's past and of the record of our men and women in peace and in war. We are confident of our country's future. We feel that our nation can hold its head high among the nations of the world.
With the pleasure we have in welcoming you of Newfoundland as Canadians there is mingled a feeling that you could have joined no better nation. The formal union is completed today. But the real union-the union of hearts and minds-took place in the recent terrible war in which Canadians and Newfoundlanders were so closely joined.
It is not only in war that we have come to know and appreciate the qualities of the people of Newfoundland. During the centuries since the original settlement of Newfoundland the people of your island have met the forces of nature, on sea and on land. In adversity and in prosperity they have developed qualities of heart and spirit for which they are renowned.
Some of those qualities are referred to by your native son E. J. Pratt, who has written: This is their culture, this-their master passion Of giving shelter and of sharing bread,
Of answering rocket signals in the fashion Of losing life to save it. In the spread Of time-the Gilbert-Grenfell-Bartlett span-
The headlines cannot dim their daily story,
Nor calls like London! Gander! Teheran!
Outplay the drama of the sled and dory.
The fact that Newfoundland has become a province of Canada will not cause you to lose your identity, of which you are all so justly proud.
A Canadian province is not a mere administrative unit of the central government. Each of our provinces has its own distinctive political existence and political traditions. Within its field of jurisdiction the provincial legislature is as sovereign as the parliament of Canada is within its field. The provincial legislature has jurisdiction over education; property and civil rights; charitable, local and municipal institutions. To the province also falls the primary responsibility for public health and social welfare.
In entrusting such jurisdiction to the province, the Fathers, in their wisdom, left to the province the primary responsibility for the protection of the family, the school, the church, the very foundations of our society.
Our constitution thus assures to each province the preservation of its ancient traditions, its own culture and all those distinctive characteristics which add variety and colour to our national life.
Newfoundland today enters confederation as a full and equal partner with the older provinces. It is my hope and belief that in the future the advantages of the union will be increasingly recognized by the great majority of the people of Newfoundland and of all Canada.
We are completing our union at a troubled time for all people who believe in freedom and democracy and who hope for peace. The free and peace-loving countries of the north Atlantic community are at the present moment taking steps, within the charter of the United Nations, to band themselves together for greater security against any would-be aggressor.
Newfoundland is in the very centre of the north Atlantic community. Canada as a whole occupies a large part of the north Atlantic area. The nations of that whole area will be more secure in the new north Atlantic association. In the same way, Canada and Newfoundland will have greater security in being bound together in federal union. From today all Canadians, old and new, will work as one to preserve peace and to win security. And in a world where free people can work in security and peace, the opportunities for the enlarged Canada, with its ten provinces, are immense.
Among our people there are some who still do not have that standard of living we think all Canadians should have. There are some who still do not enjoy an adequate degree of social security. We shall not cease to work for a larger measure of prosperity and security for all our people in all parts of Canada.
But while there is yet room for improvement, there is no country in the world where that improvement is more possible, or, indeed, more certain. The wealth of Canada is the

wealth of half a continent. The talents and the energies of our people are those of free men who work together for the benefit of all. Our wealth, our talents, our energy, and our co-operation constitute the promise of our country.
The people of Newfoundland, who have today become citizens of Canada, will share with the people of the rest of Canada in the work and in the wealth of our nation. Together we shall strive, under God's guidance and with confidence in our future, to build a greater and a better land.
In conclusion I welcome as a colleague in the government of Canada the Honourable Gordon Bradley, of Newfoundland, who this morning was sworn to the privy council and becomes Secretary of State of Canada.
(Translation):
I should like to give to the Newfoundlanders of yesterday, who are Canadians today, the assurance that, in addressing to them these words of welcome in English, I do so quite as much in the name of their new compatriots whose mother tongue is French, as in the name of those whose language is English.
They belong now to a nation whose two principal races have both retained their attachment to the traditions, to the culture, and to the language of their ancestors. That is the best guarantee to our new fellow citizens that their entry into this union will not cause them to lose their own ancestral patrimony, but that, on the contrary, it will make its contribution with ours to the common good of all Canadian citizens.

speakeroldname: Hon. F. G. Bradley (Secretary of State):
speechtext:
This is a day which will live long in North American history. It is a day of fulfilment-fulfilment of a vision of great men who planned the nation of Canada more than eighty years ago; and as we stand here on this day of destiny our thoughts fly back through the years to those far-seeing men of the past-Macdonald, Brown, and Cartier in Canada, and Carter and Shea in Newfoundland-whose vision was broader and deeper than their times, and whose conception of a united British North America has just become a reality. In fancy we can see them now, bending over this scene in silent and profound approval.
That they were right is not now open to question. The history of the Canada they began in 1867 leaves no room for doubt upon that point, and the logic of these eighty years indicates that a still greater and better Canada for us all lies in the future.
For me this day transforms a dream of long ago into an accomplished fact. For many years I have felt that our similar independence was unsound; that the close proximity of my native island to the mainland constituted a clear call for union with Canada; that the allegiance to one crown, which we have always shared with Canada, beckoned us westward; that the identity of our principles and traditions pointed in the same direction.
All these considerations led irrevocably to but one conclusion-that Macdonald, Brown and Cartier, and Carter and Shea, were right; and I am happy that this day has come in my time.
I suppose that this union will make hardly any appreciable impression upon the lives of the citizens of Canada of yesterday, but to the people of the new province the changes will be deep and abiding.
In some matters they will lose that exclusiveness of control of their own destinies which they have heretofore enjoyed, and in return they acquire a share in the councils of a great nation-the new Canada -of which they have become a part; they must accustom themselves to a new system of government-the federal system-which links them with all Canadians and yet assures them of a continuance of that identity of which they have always been so proud. They will experience new channelings of trade, new standards of social legislation, new methods of taxation, and a new measure of responsibility as citizens of the New Canada.
Confederation in the days of Macdonald was perhaps comparatively simple, but in the complexities and uncertainties of our modern world it is inevitable that in the process of adjustment to their changed status there will be stresses and strains. We shall have to meet these problems as they arise within the next few months, and perhaps the next few years; and yet out of the experience of the past we may confidently expect that they will not prove as difficult in the future.
Indeed, that process of adjustment has already begun, and we Newfoundland Canadians have been deeply impressed by the speedy recognition of our problems by those whom I may term the older Canadians, and their sincere desire to co-operate with us in effecting the transition as smoothly and with as little dislocation as possible.
Thus we begin life as one people in an atmosphere of unity. We are all Canadians now. Now, as never before, can it be said of this land that her bounds extend from sea to sea. From the eastern shores of the new province of Newfoundland to the coast of British Columbia let us go forward together with faith in the principles and tra-

ditions which we hold in common. Thus shall we grow in strength and prosperity. Thus will the prophetic vision of that great Canadian, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when he said that the twentieth century belonged to Canada, be acknowledged by the whole world.
Inscribing the Arms of Newfoundland on the Peace Tower:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The dominating feature of the capital of Canada is the tower before which we now are standing. It has become known, through visit or photograph or painting, to almost every Canadian. To Canadians it is a symbol of our confederation, and of its spirit and character.
The tower arose out of the ashes of the old parliament building which was destroyed by fire in 1916. When it was built it was dedicated to peace, and on the arch of its base were inscribed the coats of arms of the nine provinces of Canada. The architects and stonecutters charged with the work, however, carved ten shields instead of nine. One was left blank for the day, which the fathers of confederation had foreseen, when Newfoundland would join Canada. That day has come.
It is most gratifying to me as Prime Minister of Canada to cut the first line on the shield that will bear the arms of the ancient colony of Newfoundland, now the tenth province of Canada.
I do so, for my own part and on behalf of my predecessor, Mr. Mackenzie King, who as Prime Minister had a large and decisive part in bringing about the union.
I feel confident that the inscription in hard and enduring stone will not be more lasting than the union of which it is the symbol.
(These remarks repeated by Mr. St. Laurent in French.)
Address of His Excellency the Governor General
It is my privilege today in speaking to the people of Newfoundland, and to those who are now their fellow citizens in the rest of Canada, to convey a message from His Majesty the King. The message is as follows:
Please convey to the government and people of Canada on behalf of the Queen and myself our appreciation of the message of loyalty and good wishes which you sent me. On this historic occasion I am glad to send my good wishes to the people of the greater Canada-to those of the old provinces and to those of the new province of Newfoundland -who will now go forward together to the high destiny that awaits them. Today marks the fulfilment of the union into one great nation of all peoples of the British commonwealth in the northern part of North America. May the union that is now complete continue, under God's guidance, to grow in strength, prosperity, happiness, and may it bring new benefits to its people from sea to sea.
As representative of His Majesty, and as Governor General of Canada, it is a special pleasure for me to be able to convey that message on so historic an occasion.
The ceremony we have witnessed, the beginning of the carving of the arms of Newfoundland on the tenth shield in the arch of the peace tower, is a perfect symbol of the event we celebrate today. When union of the British colonies in North America was discussed at Quebec in 1864, Newfoundland was represented. At that time it was expected that Newfoundland would form a part of the proposed union. When the confederation that is now Canada was established, and Newfoundland was not included, the union was felt to be incomplete. It has remained incomplete until today.
When the arch in the peace tower was constructed, the sense of proportion of the architect confirmed the judgment of the fathers who had planned confederation. With only nine shields, no balance could be achieved that would satisfy the requirements of beauty and symmetry. And so the arch, like the union, was unfinished until the people of Newfoundland decided to join in the union which their representatives originally helped to plan. The people of Newfoundland have now so decided. The arch and the union will now be complete.
While I have not yet had occasion to visit Newfoundland, the qualities of its people are by no means unknown to me. The reputation established by the Royal Newfoundland regiment in the war of 1914-18 will always be a source of pride to the island whose sons that regiment made famous. In the last war I had under my own command in Italy the 166th (Newfoundland) Field regiment, Royal Artillery, which carried on so well the reputation established by the sons of Newfoundland in the first world war. It was, perhaps, an augury of the union being completed today that the 166th regiment was in support of the first Canadian division at Ortona in Italy.
As Governor General of Canada it is a pleasure for me to be able to welcome the people of Newfoundland into the country in which it is my privilege to represent His Majesty the King. I trust it will soon be my pleasure to visit the people of the new province in their own island and to greet again some of the gallant men who served under my command in Italy. To them, and to all the people of Newfoundland, I send today a word of greeting and of welcome as citizens of Canada.

Commentator: The Governor General and the official party are now preparing to leave the platform which has been erected on the steps of the peace tower here at the houses of parliament on parliament hill in Ottawa. The Governor General and the Prime Minister have left the platform, and Mr. King is speaking with the new Secretary of State, the Honourable Mr. Bradley.
That concludes the official ceremony from parliament hill in Ottawa, linking Newfoundland with Canada as its tenth province.
Before returning you to our studios and our regular broadcasting schedule, we shall hear from Robert Donnell, Canada's official carilloneur, who will play "This Canada of Ours", his own composition, specially written for the citizenship ceremonies held in January of 1947.
(Carillon)
The composite guard of honour, made up of members of the army and air force, commanded by Major A. E. Wood, is now preparing to leave. Incidentally this is also a great day for the air force, since today marks the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Royal Canadian Air Force. Doubtless there are many Newfoundland boys in the guard of honour.
Photographers are now taking pictures of the shield which was inscribed by the Prime Minister. During the ceremony the Prime Minister carved the first stone from the shield which will bear the coat of arms of the province of Newfoundland, one of the first to appear in the new world. The present coat of arms of Canada dates only from November, 1921, although an earlier Dominion of Canada coat of arms came into use following a royal warrant dated May 26, 1868, which coat of arms was composed merely of the four original provinces' coats of arms assigned at the time and by the same warrant.
